Multidisciplinary Curriculum and Learning Material 
The current Indian higher education system caters to curriculum that are developed and taught in 
silos. NEP envisions of a multidisciplinary and integrated curriculum that cuts across multiple 
disciplines, making the education truly interdisciplinary. However, the prevalent idea of 
multidisciplinary and interdisciplina ry in the Indian higher education system is to borrow certain 
aspects from other discipline and integrate it with the host discipline. However, NEP‟s idea of 
multidisciplinary education is to understand a problem in such a way that its solution is achieved  by 
using the knowledge of various disciplines. NEP stresses upon various pedagogical avenues such as 
critical thinking, role play, simulation, problem solving approach, and experiential learning. This 
approach takes away the superiority of alpha disciplin e. The contemporary practice of curriculum 
building is devoid of such thinking. In case higher education institutions are able to devise such 
curriculum, evaluation system emerges as another problem area. NEP necessitates continuous and 
formative evaluatio n system. Secondly, learning material, particularly textbooks, must be 
modified/rewritten accordingly. It is a big task, and institutions are not equipped to augment such 
skills. The current capacities of faculty do not gel well with the requirements stated above. 
Multi Entry and Multiple Exit (MEME) Options 

29  
NEP proposes multi -entry and multi -exit options for the students. While it looks like a flexible 
system, which is being operated by Western education institutions quite effectively, Indian institutions 
are likely to face several issues in implementing this system. Due to high population, the estimated 
intake of students in higher education every year is quite high. If institutions allow MEME, it would 
be very difficult for the institutions to predict how  many students would exit and how many would 
join midway. Since institutions would not know the in - and out-traffic, it  will certainly disturb the 
PTR. Uneven geographical distribution of higher education institutions would create hurdles in 
managing MEME in several areas, mostly countryside. The institutions have not thought very clearly 
about this problem and how they will resolve it when it is at their doorstep.

1. The Committee observes that through various appreciable activities, the implementation 
of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 is progressing on course which would surely 
fructify its vision to transform the higher education system to be more inclusive, flexible, and 
aligned with global standar ds. The Committee notes that one of the primary keys to ensure 
successful implementation of NEP  would be synergized collaboration between Government 
bodies, universities, industry partners, and civil society.  
2. The Committee appreciates the manner in whi ch the implementation of NEP and the 
vision it espouses is being taken forward by the UT of Jammu and Kashmir.  The Committee 
notes that the UT of J&K is one of the first in the country to implement NEP 2020 from the 
academic session 2022 in all the Higher  Education Institutions. It also notes that it has been at 
the forefront in implementing NEP by bringing significant changes in the assessment system 
from rote learning to a competency based learning. Also, a paradigm shift in the methods of 
teaching in class room to learn from surroundings in order to give holistic and lifelong learning 
opportunities to students is being witnessed across J&K which will ensure sustained training of 
students as global citizens with 21st century skills and create a vibrant, i nnovative, practical 
and vocational skill set and research-oriented, learner-centric education system in our country.  
3. The Committee is pleased to note that the University of Jammu has recently been 
designated as the nodal University by the University G rants Commission (UGC) to spearhead 
the implementation of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 in the Union Territory of 
Jammu and Kashmir as this distinction brings great pride and honour to the institution. Noting 
that the University of Jammu has been entrusted with the pivotal responsibility of executing the 
mandates set forth in the NEP, along with various recommendations and regulations outlined 

45  
by the UGC, the Committee hopes that with this new role, the University of Jammu will be able 
play a central role in creating awareness, arranging programs, and offering guidance to higher 
education institutions within Jammu and Kashmir to effectively implement NEP, thereby 
providing a platform to exchange and adopt best practices.  
4. The Committee takes note and appreciates the introduction of "Design Your Degree"  
based on Choice Based Credit System(CBCS)  launched by Jammu University under which 
students will be offered an opportunity to craft a personalized, interdisciplinary learning 
experience. The Committee further observes that "Design Your Degree" will also be introduced 
in Kashmir University, IUST Awantipora, ICSC Srinagar, GCW Parade Jammu, which is 
commendable. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should take 
initiatives for in troduction of "Design Your Degree" programme in various other HEIs  in the 
country, as a model contemporary and futuristic in the interest of the student community and 
nation readiness. It will to enable the students to craft a personalized, interdisciplina ry learning 
experience. 
 
5. The Committee is of the view that under the Rashtriya Uchchatar Shiksha Abhiyan 
(RUSA) Scheme, strategic funding to higher educational institutions based on critical appraisal 
of State’s higher educational plans which describe e ach State’s strategy to address issues of 
equity, access and excellence in higher education can go a long way in pushing NEP ’s aims. Key 
features of the Scheme like up -gradation of existing autonomous colleges to universities, 
conversion of colleges to cluster colleges with revamping the curriculum, skill development, 
examination reform, upgrading institutions to higher level and strategic funding should be the 
special focus of the UGC. 
6. The Committee hopes that the steps that the Department is taking as per NEP will be 
able to actively enhance engagement  and find a connect with the industry and Higher 
Educational Institutions (HEIs), through which they can experiment, pitch ideas and deploy 
them bringing a close alignment in the practices of academia  thereby synchronizing innovation 
research with the need of the time and industry to achieve objective of real change. 
7. The Committee appreciates the steady progress in the field of higher education. The 
committee recommends that the specific impetus is required to be assigned to factors which can 
help the country’s ranking in patent filing  though the overall patent filing has improved 

46  
significantly but more needs to be done by enhanced allocation for Anusandhan (Research).  
8. The Committee appreciates the  manner in which the NEP 2020 places thrust on 
developing a student’s ‘Creative Potential’ based on higher -order cognitive capacities and to 
cultivate innovation and creativity in learners through industry -institution linkages and 
collaborative programme. Noting that the NEP prioritizes research and innovation with 
financial commitment to academic research , the Committee observes that promoting thought -
provoking research is a pre -requisite for outstanding education and will surely transform India 
into a vibrant knowledge society.  
9. The Committee appreciates that the freedom being given to Indian universities to set up 
campuses in other countries and initiate start -up incubation centers, technology development 
centers and centers in frontier areas of research helps foster knowledge creation and innovation 
which will contribute to the growing national economy. In this regard the Committee also takes 
note of G20 New Delhi declaration that supported promoting open, equitable, and secure 
scientific collaborat ion and encouraging mobility of students, scholars, researchers 
and scientists across research and higher education institutions. The Declaration also 
emphasized on expanding access to high -quality technical and vocational education 
and training. The Committee is of the view that the expected benefits through these initiatives 
call for commitment of all stakeholders, be it the Department, regulatory bodies or Universities , 
educationists, and industries,  so that , these innovative strategies in the areas of s kill 
development, upskilling and entrepreneurship bring the expected boost to create a knowledge 
society that contributes to global education , hence global good.  The Committee further 
recommends that efforts, in unison, by both the Central and S tate Governments, would be 
necessary for successful implementation and sustenance of these policies and schemes.  
10. Noting that the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020initiates several significant 
reforms to transform higher education in the country by promoting q uality, relevance, and 
innovation in higher education, the Committee appreciates the various steps to promote the use 
of digital technologies in education, including the development of digital libraries & SWAYAM 
PRABHA portal . It is of the view that the recommendation for the creation of a National 
Educational Technology Forum (NETF) to equip students with the skills and knowledge 
necessary to contribute to the nation’s development and compete in the global job market can 

47  
go a long way in e xpansion of digital infrastructure to make the country a Global Knowledge 
Hub thereby enhancing domain area of digital infrastructure, content and capacity building. 
11. The Committee observes that there is going to be significant i mpact of Digital Libraries 
on Knowledge Ecosystem  as part of the NEP’s digitization agenda, digital libraries will play a 
crucial role in providing online access to an extensive range of digital resources, such as e -
books, journals, articles, and multimedia content.  These online platforms will enable students 
and educators to conveniently connect with educational materials at any time and from any 
location, while also offering a cost -effective means of providing the permit to top -notch 
educational content.  The commit tee recommends that the department must ensure that the 
content on digital library should also be available in regional languages for better reach out and 
learning outcome.   
12. The Committee recommends that the Department and related stakeholders should 
prioritize the implementation of digital initiatives to ensure that every student, regardless of 
their background or location, has reach to quality education. In addition, policies that 
encourage the adoption of digital technologies in education should be framed, and both students 
and teachers should be provided adequate training for their use.  
 13. The Committee also recommends that requisite efforts be made  so that these knowledge 
ecosystems carry flexibility so that it can  be tailored to fit the unique learning requirements of 
individual students, allowing them to learn at their own pace and in a style that suits them best , 
so that , Digital libraries offer a cost -effective means of accessing high -quality educational 
content, which can help to lower the o verall cost of education and make it more accessible and 
affordable to a wider range of students.  
14.  The Committee is of the view that proper involvement of the student community, 
incorporation of their feedback and suggestions towards the changes propo sed in NEP will help 
institutions in orienting students faster and in a more effective way which will be helpful in 
creating institutional mechanisms to handle student ’s  queries on issues such as Academic Bank 
of Credits (ABC), Multiple Entry and Exit sys tem and generate beneficial results in terms of 
acceptance and smoother implementation.  In the early stages the learning has to be a both way 
process for a substantive evolution and successful implementation. 
15. The Committee is of the view that t echnology can play a pivotal role in accelerating the 

48  
implementation of initiatives outlined in NEP 2020 in higher education institutions in India. The 
Committee recommends that by adopting and harnessing the power of modern cloud based 
technologies with a malgamation of data,  higher education institutions can create a more 
efficient, transparent, and student -centric ecosystem. These technologies have the potential to 
revolutionize credentialing, personalize learning, improve student outcomes, streamline 
administrative processes, enhance research capabilities, and foster innovation. Integrating 
technology aligns with the vision of NEP 2020, promoting a future -ready education system that 
equips students with the skills and knowledge needed in the 21st century. 
16. The Committee notes and appreciates the emphasis that the National Education Policy 
2020 (NEP) places on internationalisation stating that ‘High performing Indian universities will 
be encouraged to set up campuses in other countries, and similarly, se lected universities e.g., 
those from among the top 100 universities in the world will be facilitated to operate in India’. 
Further the Committee appreciates that the UGC’s draft regulations on ‘Setting up and 
Operation of Foreign Higher Educational Institutions in India’ have been issued which is a good 
step forward in the entire reform process.  
18. Taking note of some of the observations of IRMA, the Committee is of the view that the 
successful implementation of initiatives to enhance access to education for marginalized 
communities is not only a moral imperative but also essenti al for the inclusive and sustainable 
development so that education becomes a powerful tool for uplifting all segments of society, 
regardless of their socio -economic status or background. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends for implementation of certain sp ecific initiatives aimed at enhancing access to 
education for marginalized communities in accordance with the National Education Policy 
(NEP) 2020 so that its thrust on inclusivity and equitability for all segments of society gets 
requisite boost:  . 
i. Comprehensive Awareness Campaigns: Launch comprehensive awareness campaigns 
targeting marginalized communities to inform them about the importance of education 
and the opportunities provided by the NEP 2020. These campaigns should be conducted 
in local languages and dialects, utilizing various media channels including television, 
radio, print, and social media. Collaboration with local community leaders and 
organizations to maximize outreach would also be helpful. 
ii. Infrastructure Development : Invest in build ings and upgrading educational 

49  
infrastructure in underserved areas, with  particular focus on remote villages and urban 
slums. Ensure that schools are accessible, safe, and well -equipped to provide quality 
education. Allocate sufficient funds to address th e specific needs of schools catering to 
marginalized communities. 
iii. Teacher Training and Recruitment : Develop specialized training programs for teachers 
who work in marginalized communities. These programs should emphasize inclusive and 
culturally sensitive teaching methods, as well as provide incentives to attract qualified 
educators to these areas. Implement a transparent and efficient teacher recruitment 
process that prioritizes diversity. 
iv. Scholarship and Financial Support: Establish a robust scholarship and financial support 
system to mitigate economic barriers to education. Scholarships should be designed to 
address the unique needs of marginalized communities, including those from 
economically disadvantaged backgrounds, scheduled castes, scheduled tribe s, and other 
vulnerable groups. Streamline the application process to make it user -friendly and 
accessible. 
v. Digital Inclusivity: Recognize the importance of digital education in the current context 
and work towards providing marginalized communities with a ccess to digital resources. 
Equip schools with computer labs and ensure affordable internet connectivity in these 
area 
vi. Develop and distribute educational content tailored to local needs and languages. 
vii. Community Engagement : Encourage active involvement of t he local community in the 
education process. Establish Parent -Teacher Associations (PTAs) and involve them in 
institution decision-making. Promote community-driven initiatives to support education, 
such as adult literacy programs and community libraries. 
viii. Monitoring and Evaluation : Implement a robust monitoring and evaluation system to 
track the progress and impact of initiatives aimed at enhancing access to education for 
marginalized communities. Regularly collect data on enrollment, attendance, and 
learning outcomes, disaggregated by demographic factors,  and disseminate it to identify 
areas needing improvement. 
ix. Policy Adaptation: Continuously review and adapt policies to address the evolving needs 
and challenges faced by marginalized communities. Establish a feedback mechanism that 
allows stakeholders from these communities to provide input and suggestions for policy 
improvements. 

50  
x. Collaboration and Partnerships : Foster collaborations with Non-Governmental 
Organizations (NGOs), civil society organizations, an d international agencies that have 
expertise in promoting education for marginalized communities. Leverage their 
resources and knowledge to enhance the effectiveness of education initiatives. 
xi. Research and Innovation: Encourage research and innovation in the field of education 
for marginalized communities. Support studies that identify best practices and 
innovative approaches to address the unique challenges faced by these communities in 
accessing quality education. 
19. The Committee notes that addressing the issue of technological readiness and digital 
infrastructure is necessary for complying with the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020's 
requirements related to credit transfer, multidisciplinary learning, and ensuring inclusive 
education, especially for  differently-abled children. As NEP 2020 envisions a digitally 
empowered society through education, it is imperative that technology plays a pivotal role in 
facilitating these goals. In order to address the issue, the Committee recommends that the 
Department should set up a monitoring group, drawing experts from all stakeholders to 
conduct a comprehensive assessment of the current technological infrastructure in higher 
education institutions across the country, identify gaps in terms of hardware, software, internet 
connectivity, digital literacy among students and faculty and suggest solution to bridge any issue 
relating to  Technological Gaps , Investment in Digital Infrastructure , , faculty  Training and 
Development, Learning Resources, Tech Integration etc.  
20. The Committee observes that implementation of the Multi Entry and Multiple Exit 
(MEME) options within the framework of the National Education Policy (NEP) is a vital 
component of NEP 2020, offering students greater flexibility and choice in their edu cational 
pathways. In order to ensure its smooth operation, the Committee recommends that the 
Department should develop comprehensive guidelines and a well -defined framework for 
MEME options including specific eligibility criteria, credit transfer mechanisms providing clear 
roadmap for students pursuing different exit points. Also, implementation of a standardized 
Credit Accumulation and Transfer (CAT) system that allows students to earn and transfer 
credits seamlessly across institutions would facilitate smooth transitions between different levels 
of education, from certificate courses to doctoral programs.  In this regard the Committee 
appreciates the introduction of Academic Bank of Credit(ABC) in the higher education system . 
It is commendable that already more than 50% of the Universities in the country are now on -

51  
board. The Committee recommends the Department to strive for bringing on -board the 
remaining Universities and other Higher Education Institutions of the country under Academic 
Bank of Credit. 
21. The Committee is of the view that efforts towards improving the effectiveness and 
impact of the Higher Education Financing Agency (HEFA) in playing a crucial role in funding 
and supporting higher education institutions would prove beneficial. Towa rds this aim, the 
Committee recommends that HEFA can consider diversifying its funding sources beyond 
Government allocations, explore partnerships with private sector organizations, philanthropic 
foundations, and international financial institutions to inc rease the available funds. Also,  
collaboration with higher education institutions to create long -term investment plans that align 
with their strategic goals and national educational priorities besides ensuring that investments 
are directed toward areas tha t enhance academic quality, research capabilities, and student 
outcomes can be promoted.  
22. The Committee also recommends  reviewing and adjusting the interest rates on loans 
provided by HEFA to make them more competitive and affordable for institutions s o that grace 
periods or lower interest rates can be offered for institutions facing financial challenges.The 
Committee further suggests for allocating a portion of HEFA funds specifically for research and 
innovation grants to incentivize institutions to un dertake cutting -edge research and 
development projects and foster a culture of innovation within higher education. 
23. The Committee recommends the Department and UGC to expedite the process of 
engagement of "Professor of Practice" in HEIs as envisaged in the National Education Policy 
2020 to ensure greater collaboration between academia and industry for promoting holistic and 
multidisciplinary education with focus on creativity, innovation and employability. 
 
24.The Committee appreciates the following effo rts taken by department to introduce Indian 
Knowledge System(IKS) in higher education as envisaged by NEP 2020. 
(i) AICTE has permitted 41 Engineering Courses in 8 regional languages 
(ii) MBBS Course has been started in Hindi 
(iii) Common University Entrance Test conducted in 13 Languages and participated 
by 90 Universities. 

52  
(iv) JEE(Mains) and NEET(UG) conducted in 13 languages across the country. 
(v) Provision of awarding minor degree to students who completes 18 to 20 credits in 
IKS has been made. 
(vi) Funded 36 high end inte rdisciplinary research projects (Calls for up to 70 
research projects in 9 thematic areas are out now and results will be declared 
on30th November, 2022). 
(vii) More than 25 IKS Centers have been established 
(viii) 64 high end interdisciplinary research projects are undergoing 
(ix) More than 8000 HEIs have started adopting IKS into their curriculum and 
digitization of 1.5Lakhsbooks. 
 
25. The Committee observes that in order to attain the targets of Atma Nirbhar Bharat and 
to develop an Institutional Research Information Sy stem for sharing the status of 
ongoing/completed projects/programmes, expertise and resources etc.  making effective use of 
Information and Communication Technology for preparing the database of in -house experts to 
provide industrial consultancy and service s, 542 Higher Education Institutions including 244 
Universities and 298 colleges have established R&D cells at their campuses.  The Committee 
recommends the Department to take special efforts and provide budgetary and infrastructure 
support to set up R&D ce lls in all Universities of the country and other Higher Education 
Institutions(HEIs) in a time -bound manner to contribute in the making of  Atma Nirbhar  
Bharat. 
 
26. The Committee observes and appreciates that there has been a gradual increase in the 
Gross Enrollment Ratio (GER) for all students and it has risen from 24.1% in 2016-17 to 27.3% 
in 2020-21. The Committee further observes that GER for ST and SC students has also risen 
from 2016-17 to 2020 -21.The GER for ST students also increased from 20.3% to 2 3.1%, while 
the GER for SC students increased from 14.8% to 18.9% . The committee also appreciates the 
efforts of the department like SWAYAM PRABHA &Massive Open Online Courses(MOOCs) 
in order to achieve a robust GER.   
 
27. The Committee observes that 42 p ercent of universities, 36 percent of colleges and 22 
percent of stand -alone institutions have connectivity with National Mission on Education 
through Information and Communication Technology (NMEICT)  and their connectivity with 

53  
National Knowledge Network (NKN) is 56, 89, and 24percent respectively. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that efforts should be made to ensure connectivity with the NKM and 
NMEICT for all remaining Universities& Higher Education Institutes(HEIs) in the country. 
 
28. As per the N EP 2020, regulatory bodies i.e. UGC and AICTE, the Pupil Teacher Ratio 
(PTR) in higher education is required to be kept at healthy level . The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the department should fulfill the vacancies in a time bound manner to 
maintain the prescribed PTR. 
 
29. The Committee takes note of the issues and difficulties in implementing the Multi Entry 
and Multiple Exit (MEME) Options. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department to 
have wider consultation with various Universities/Institutions, their regulatory bodies and other 
stakeholders to devise out way in view of the difficulties being faced in implementing Multi 
Entry and Multiple Exit (MEME) Options and apprise the Committee of the same. 
 
30. The Committee takes note of the fact that banks can-not enforce SARFAESI Act in case 
of default by borrower as same may jeopardize the careers of students  (As per the submission 
given by the banks) . The Committee, recommends that banks must take note of the Credit 
Guarantee Fund Scheme for Education Loan (CGFSEL) launched by the Department of Higher 
Education, Govt. of India in 2015 which provides a guarantee of education loan up to INR 7.5 
Lakhs. The Committee also recommends that the Ministry of Education in consultation with the 
Ministry of Finance should look into a proposal to increase the guarantee amount under this 
scheme.

society, based out of the National Law School of India University, Bangalore.  The Consortium conducts the 
CLAT.  The current status of the CLAT exam is that it is the exclusive mode of admission to 22 National 
Law Universities as well as more than 75 other institutions, which include private law colleges and various 
other institutions, including the Indian Army and various PSUs which use it as a selection exam.  It was then 
informed that it is the largest law examination in the country and has been growing year on year. In 2022, 
NLSIU conducted the exam for CLAT, 2023 and they have announced the results within one week and have 
begun the counseling.  Also, two rounds of counseling were over in January, 2023.   
25. The Committee was then informed that law post-graduates are about 1,300 and almost 99 per cent of 
these seats are already filled.  The last round of counseling would be in May, 2023, where NLSIU will close 
the final round and apart from the Common Law Admission Test, which is the largest exam, NLU, Delhi 
conducts a separate test.   
26. The representatives of DCI in their presentation submitted that examination for admission to dental 
courses, BDS is similar to NMC and is being conducted by NTA along with MBBS.  NEET-MDS is also 
conducted by National Board of Examination which was usually held by 10th May and the result is declared 
by 1st week of June, 2023.  
27. The representatives of Pharmacy Council of India apprised the Committee that this year GPAT and 
EXIT Exam would be held. Also, it was informed that GPAT till date is being conducted by AICTE but 
from next year, it would be conducted by Pharmacy Council of India. It was also informed that problem 
relating to stipend which is provided by AICTE as PCI has no such provision for providing stipend. It was 
also informed that previously 4,000 colleges were there but now 2,400 new colleges have been added. While 
replying to a query regarding entrance exams for PCI, it was informed that admission committee prepares a 
merit list according to percentage of twelfth class exams and initiates the admission process thereon.

Report1. Provisions of NEP-2020 relating to Research based Education1.1 NEP, 2020 recognizes that the world is undergoing rapid changes in the knowledgelandscape. Moreover, the Committee emphasizes the need for adequate funding towards research endeavors aimed at identifying scientific and practical solutions for addressing societal, developmental, financial, and techno-economic challenges, aligning with the objectives outlined in the Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF). Internationally renowned universities cover these costs, including infrastructure development and maintenance, through overheads or indirect costs on research grants. The Committee, therefore, stresses that it is imperative by the concerned Ministries/ Departments to reconsider the overheads provided on public-funded research projects as the current rate falls significantly short of meeting the actual operational expenses which impedes the progress and affordability of research initiatives. In light of this, the Committee strongly recommends that funding agencies for scientific research, such as the Department of Science and Technology, Department of Biotechnology, Department of Higher Education, etc. should allocate additional funds for the development and maintenance of physical infrastructure, including laboratories, computational resources, equipment and machineries in particular and other facilities, for all publicly funded research projects in various scientific disciplines. Further, internships, joint projects, and mentorship programs which can foster practical skills and knowledge and organize seminars, workshops, and outreach programs should also be encouraged to generate interest in space science among the public and attract morestudents to pursue careers in this field.6.19 The Committee recommends that the University Grants Commission (UGC) shouldtake a focused approach through formulation of a blueprint to bolster the research scenario in India and the following points be examined in light of current policies while developing the proposed blueprint: mechanisms to encourage a robust research culture across universities by incentivizing and recognizing research contributions, developing schemes that reward quality publications, patents, and impactful research outcomes.increase funding specifically earmarked for research activities within Universities, facilitate grants for research projects, infrastructure development, and faculty development programs.foster an environment conducive to interdisciplinary research by encouraging collaborations among departments and institutions and establishing more interdisciplinary research centers to tackle complex challenges requiring diverse expertise.

Government for improving the research scenario in the country in the field of science, technology

has taken numerous efforts to enhance the Research & Development (R&D) expenditure and create 
adequate opportunities for the researchers. It has also taken various steps to increase opportunities 
for research students pursuing Ph.D. and postdoctoral research and its efforts is visible through its 
global position in scientific publications, number of Ph.Ds., number of start-ups, resident patent 
filing, Global Innovation Index, etc. during the last three years. The Committee was also informed 
that India occupies 3rd rank in terms of number of scientific publications, number of Ph.Ds. 
awarded and number of start-ups. India is ranked at 7th position in terms of resident patent filing

Universities to the meeting of the Committee and asked them to apprise the Committee on 
"Anusandhan scenario in Sciences and related fields along with Industry 4.0 and Emerging

The Committee desired to be apprised of the strategies adopted/ steps taken by the Government for 
improving the research scenario in the country in the field of science, technology and innovations, 
details of the fund allocated, released and utilized by the Department for promotion and 
augmentation of research in various sciences in the country, along with the hindrances and 
difficulties being faced in making India a world leader in the field of science and emerging 
technologies such as Artificial Intelligence, Internet of Things, Blockchain technology. Then 
Committee decided to hear the views of Directors and Vice-Chancellor of various Institutes/ 
Universities to begin with the meeting. 
6. The Director, IIST, Thiruvananthapuram started his deposition by informing the Committee 
of the undergraduate courses, one dual degree and 15 post graduate programmes along with doctor 
programmes in various areas of Space Science and Technology in IIST. He further informed that 
institute has an NIRF ranking of 48 in the year 2023 and 1,316 graduates who passed out of IIST 
are serving in ISRO and they have come up to the middle level management and toppers from the 
institute do masters programme in Caltech, the prestigious university in the US and several 
students have completed their internships at Jet Propulsion Laboratory, USA and IIST is going to

collaboration with more than 10 international institutions and more than 30 national institutions to 
develop technologies that will be feeding to ISRO and also for many societal applications.

achievements of the institute in field of nanotechnology like development of single sheet Boron 
technology. He informed the Committee about the cancer drug discovery which has been a major 
research in which the relation of a type of bacteria, H-Pylori bacteria with cancer has been 
established.

no. 1 in the NIRF rankings under the university category, under the Research Institutions category 
and has been ranked as the world's top research university in terms of Citations per Faculty in the 
latest QS World University Rankings. He then informed that IISc has developed techniques for 
assessing the emotional and skill development of autistic children using AI techniques because the 
autistic children do not interact with human beings. He then informed that using IoT by appropriate 
sensing technology, we are able to develop much more efficient water distribution mechanisms.  
 9.  Acting Director, IIT Bombay, Maharashtra, informed the Committee that IIT, Bombay has 
about 85 faculty members across all Departments who work in AI in every branch of science, 
engineering, etc. and therefore, IIT has created a Centre for Machine Intelligence and Data Science 
about three-plus years back, and this Centre, along with the faculty from all the Departments, 
works in many areas such as is healthcare and life science. 
10. Director, IIT Indore, apprised the Committee that there are 9 under-graduate programmes 
and 16 post-graduate programmes in the Institute.  About 600 Ph.D. students work in the Institute 
and we have more than 2,800 total number of students in the Institute.  IIT Indore stands 14th in 
NIRF Ranking in the country. He then informed the Committee of the various on-going projects in 
field of Artificial Intelligence, agriculture and disaster management being initiated by the 
institution.  
11.  Director, IISER, Mohali, Punjab, informed that IISER focuses in providing very high level and 
integrated education on basic sciences of Physics, Chemistry, Biology and Maths combining it 
with research at the same time.  He further informed that the first five institutions were set up 
between 2006 and 2008 at Kolkata, Pune, Mohali, Thiruvananthapuram and Bhopal.

such as intrinsically disordered proteins, stem cells and their relationship to disease development, 
particularly with regard to development of heart and blood vessels, ultra fast lasers and high 
powered lasers in collaboration with DRDO and low cost system for domestic waste water 
management. 
12.  Director, Research Development, Assam University informed the Committee that the 
university has two campuses, one at Silchar and another at Diphu. It was also informed that Assam 
University has 43 Academic Departments out of which 27 Departments are for humanities and 
social sciences and Management.  Also, it has three Engineering Departments and 11 Science 
Departments along with Pharmacy.  There are 79 affiliated colleges where nearly 60,000 students 
are studying. He also apprised the Committee that the university is creating its own resources for 
research purposes and in 2021-22, it has received 65 projects from 22 funding agencies amounting 
to Rs.13.5 crore.  While, in 2020-21, it was 50 projects from 18 agencies.  The institute is also 
working well to carry on nano research consortiums. Our computer scientists and engineering 
faculties are working in AI block chain and IoT, mainly in the field of agriculture as we are having 
one Agricultural Engineering Department within North-East Region. With regard to research and

schools, 26 departments and 34 courses are running. There are teachers and students from 28 
States, so this university gives a view of the entire mini India.

POSHAN ABHIYAAN 
Recommendation 
4. The Committee while noting the above measures appreciates the technological interventions 
in collecting the data related to Anganwadi Services and Poshan Abhiyaan on real time basis. The 
Committee, accordingly, keeping in view the fact that since this Integrated Nutrition Support aims at 
improving the nutritional and health status in children, adolescent girls, pregnant women and 
lactating mothers and addresses the challenges of malnutrition, recommends that the Ministry must 
closely monitor the progress of the Scheme in the States and impress upon them to prioritize these 
welfare schemes so that benefits reach the needy. 
(Para 3.2.15 ibid) 
Action Taken 
In order to closely monitor the progress of the scheme, a robust ICT enabled platform named 
Poshan tracker has been designed to capture near real-time data on implementation and monitoring of 
POSHAN Abhiyaan across the country. The Poshan Tracker management application monitors 
activities at the Anganwadi Centre (AWC) including service deliveries of Anganwadi Workers 

9 
 
(AWWs) and thereby facilitates complete beneficiary management. Around 10.11 crore beneficiaries 
are registered under the Poshan Tracker and more than 94% are Aadhaar verified.  
The Poshan Tracker also enables better coordination and communication between AWWs 
and supervisors. The supervisors can access the data remotely and provide guidance or feedback to 
the AWWs. This improves the quality of service delivery and ensures that beneficiaries receive the 
necessary support promptly. To ensure last mile tracking of service delivery SMS alerts to 
beneficiaries has been introduced for delivery of Take Home Ration (not raw ration). Further, a 
Poshan Helpline operationalised in November 2022 has been made available for registering 
concerns. Through the help line, a beneficiary can raise a concern or a query about the services 
offered under Mission Poshan 2.0. 
In order to make the programme more effective and to ensure that all benefits including 
supplementary nutrition should reach to the intended beneficiaries, Government has taken steps to 
strengthen nutritional content, delivery outreach and outcomes with focus on developing practices 
that nurture health, wellness and immunity to disease and malnutrition. Steps have been taken to 
improve nutritional quality and testing in accredited labs, strengthen delivery and leverage 
technology to improve governance. In this regard, Streamlined Guidelines were issued on 
13.01.2021, covering several aspects such as quality assurance, roles and responsibilities of duty 
holders, procedure for procurement, integrating AYUSH concepts and Data management and 
monitoring through “Poshan Tracker” for transparency, efficiency and accountability in delivery of 
Supplementary Nutrition has been issued. Under these guidelines, the District Magistrate (DM) has 
been designated as the Nodal Point in the district for monitoring nutritional status and quality 
standards.  
Besides State Level Committees under Chief Secretaries are mandated to monitor the 
outcomes of the scheme in convergence with line departments. Further, vide Poshan 2.0 guidelines, 
States/UTs have been advised with respect to the following- 
 To ensure dietary diversity and last mile delivery of Take Home Ration to the beneficiary.  
 Preparation of Take Home Ration using locally available and culturally appropriate food 
ingredients. 

10 
 
 To delineate the Take Home Ration products that are being delivered to target beneficiaries 
based on their nutritional requirements such as severely acutely malnourished children 
(SAM), adolescent girls in the age group of 14-18 years, pregnant women and lactating 
mothers, besides children aged 6 months to 3 years. 
 To mandatorily provide millets as part of supplementary nutrition, at least once a week in 
palatable form

POSHAN ABHIYAAN 
Recommendation 
5. The Committee further states that the spread of Covid and subsequent lockdowns have made 
programmes like Poshan 2.0 even more important as the pandemic has brought serious economic 
and social welfare challenges for the country and especially for the economically weaker sections 
of the society. Thus, such nutritional programmes require a strong push. Besides enhanced 
budgetary support, successful implementation would require sustained monitoring and a combined 
multi-sectoral approach. State-specific time bound strategies which take into account various 
socioeconomic factors, sectors and dimensions of nutrition be also incorporated in the roadmap. 
 
(Para 3.2.16 ibid) 
Action Taken 
The Minister has informed that Saksham Anganwadi and Mission Poshan 2.0 (hereinafter 
referred to as Saksham Anganwadi) aim to address Government’s commitment to address the 
challenge of child malnutrition and maternal under-nutrition through a strategic shift in nutrition 

22 
 
content and delivery and create conditions and a convergent eco-system to develop practices that 
nurture health, wellness and immunity.  
With a view to address various gaps and shortcomings in the on-going nutrition programme 
and to improve implementation as well as to accelerate improvement in nutrition and child 
development outcomes, the existing scheme components have been re-organized under Poshan 2.0 
into the primary verticals given below: 
 Nutrition Support for POSHAN through Supplementary Nutrition Programme (SNP) for 
children of the age group of 06 months to 6 years, pregnant women and lactating mothers 
(PWLM); and for Adolescent Girls in the age group of 14 to 18 years in Aspirational Districts 
and North Eastern Region (NER); 
 Early Childhood Care and Education [3-6 years] and early stimulation for (0-3 years); 
 Anganwadi Infrastructure including modern, upgraded Saksham  Anganwadi; and 
 Poshan Abhiyaan 
The objectives of Poshan 2.0 are as follows:  
 To contribute to human capital development of the country; 
 Address challenges of malnutrition; Promote nutrition awareness and good eating habits for 
sustainable health and wellbeing; and 
 Address nutrition related deficiencies through key strategies. 
Poshan 2.0 focuses on Maternal Nutrition, Infant and Young Child Feeding Norms, Treatment 
Protocols for SAM/MAM and Wellness through AYUSH practices to reduce wasting and under-
weight prevalence besides stunting and anaemia, supported by the ‘Poshan Tracker’, a new, robust 
ICT centralised data system which is being linked with the RCH Portal (Anmol) of MoHFW. 
Under POSHAN Abhiyaan to ensure effective Convergence at State level, the Chief Secretary is 
required to chair the Convergence Action Plan (CAP) meeting on quarterly basis. Similarly, 
DC/DMs also need to take CAP meetings on quarterly basis.

The Ministry has informed that prior to implementation of Mission Shakti, umbrella scheme

ROLE OF NEHRU YUVA KENDRA SANGATHAN IN COMBATING DRUG/SUBSTANCE 
ABUSE 
 
Recommendation  
1. The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the NYKS for taking out 1,65,232 youth out of the 
clutches of drug addiction and substance abuse and bringing them back to normal life style through Fit 
India Movement and have been able to bring out so many youth through this programme in the financial 
year 2021-22 by conducting this programme. The Committee, therefore, recommends that volunteers of 
NYKS through their Centres should be groomed to provide de-addiction counseling to drug addicted 
youths especially in bordering districts of India and other districts of the country which are affected by 
drug menace in collaboration with Ministry of Home Affairs and respective State Governments on regular 
basis especially in view of the menace acquiring a mammoth proportion.         (para 2.2.5) 
 
Action Taken 
The Department in its reply has submitted that it has taken note of the recommendations of the 
committee for compliance. In this regard, NYKS has proposed a programme namely “Preventive 
Education and Awareness Program on Drug and Substance Abuse” in its proposed Annual Action Plan 
for the year 2023-24. The aim is to educate and raise awareness about the dangers of drug and substance 
abuse. Through workshops and outreach campaigns, the program will provide vital information on the 
harmful effects of drugs and substance abuse and the importance of prevention of such menace among 
adolescents and youth. Healthcare Experts and practicing professional counselors in the fields of drug de-
addiction will be roped in as Resource Persons for sharing their experiences during the Programme. This 
will raise awareness among youth and adolescents and also provide vital clue and feedback for 
developing comprehensive strategies for requisite intervention and support.

name of NYVs as Jan Mitra, that volunteers under NYC scheme were earlier known as National Youth 
Corps. Subsequently, the nomenclature of National Youth Corps was revised as National Youth

between NYK and Youth Clubs at Village level and their novel volunteering work towards nation 
building is getting recognition   by their name National Youth Volunteer (NYV) under NYC- a Central 
Sector Scheme. In view of the fact that nomenclature of NYC (National Youth Corps) volunteers has 
already been revised in 2016, the Committee are requested to reconsider their

 The Committee observes that it is imperative for NYKS to establish linkage between

The Committee recommends that the Department of Youth Affairs should pursue the matter 
proactively with Ministry of Finance for additional requisite resources to develop NYKs in each 
district as District Youth Resource Centre (DYRC) and One Stop Centre for Youth at the earliest 
and keep the Committee apprised regarding outcome of the same. 
 
Recommendation  
3. The Committee notes that NYKS has requisite infrastructure and an impressive presence across 
623 districts of the country. The Committee therefore, recommends that Ministry of Youth Affairs and 
Sports should take up with Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship to develop and promote 
NYKs for the skilling, re-skilling, up-skilling and experiential learning of aspiring youth. Further, the 
Department should strive to collaborate with Ministry of Labour and Employment to develop NYKS as 
employment gateways in each district of the country. 
(para 2.3.6) 
Action Taken 
The Department has informed that as per Allocation of Business Rules the subject of skill 
development and entrepreneurship is with a different Ministry. The views of Committee are being 
intimated to Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship. 
 
Comments of the Committee  
The Committee had recommended that the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports should 
take up the matter with the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship to develop and 
promote NYKs for skilling, re-skilling, up skilling and experimental learning of youths.  The 
Committee further had also recommended that Department should strive to collaborate with 
Ministry of Labour and Employment to develop NYKs as employment gateways in each district of 
the country. 
However, Ministry in response to above recommendations has informed the Committee that 
as per Allocation of Business Rules, the subject of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship is with 
a different Ministry and i.e. Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship and the view of 
the Committee is being intimated to them.  
The Committee is aware of the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961. 
The Committee also takes note of the action taken by Ministry vis-a-vis its recommendations.  
However, the Committee invites attention of the Ministry towards Constitutional provision of 
"Collective Responsibility" of Ministries/Departments of Government. Further, the Ministry is 
silent about collaboration with Ministry of Labour and Employment to develop NYKS as 
employment gateways in each district of the country. The Committee, therefore, recommends to 
proactively pursue both the parts of recommendation with Ministry of Skill Development and 
Entrepreneurship and Ministry of Labour and Employment and keep the Committee apprised 
regarding the outcome. 

8 
 
Further, given the wide range of schemes run by various Ministries -the startup Incubation 
Centres, Mentorship programs, Skill India, Atal Innovation Mission, Pradhan Mangtri Kaushal 
Vikas Yojana- it is imperative for the Department  to align these schemes and make them accessible 
to the youth.  Moreover, the Committee also observes that given their wide social reach and 
geographic dispersion, NYKs are well-poised to undertake this role, and create opportunities for 
greater collaboration with Government and Civil Society organizations in the future.   
 
Recommendation  
4. The Committee further recommends that Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports should set up 'Girl 
Child Specific NYK Centres' in each district of the country to provide equal opportunity to girl child for 
their upskilling and to ensure employment opportunity to girls in collaboration with Ministry of Skill 
Development and Ministry of Labour and Employment. 
(para 2.3.7)

The Department has stated that priority to girls/women will be emphasized in District Youth 
Resource Centres (DYRCs) in future collaboration programmes with Ministry of Skill Development and 
Entrepreneurship (MSDE), so that focused attention may be given to the female population in terms of 
employment, skilling and education. Ministry of Labour & Employment shall also be consulted for the 
same. 
 
Comments of the Committee  
The Committee observes that the Department has not taken up the matter of setting up of 
'Girl Child specific NYK Centers', so far, with the Ministry of Skill Development and 
Entrepreneurship and Ministry of Labour and Employment.  The Committee, therefore, reiterates 
its recommendation at Para 2.3.7 of its 354th Report that the Ministry should expedite the issue to 
provide equal opportunity to girl child for their upskilling and ensuring employment opportunity 
for them. The Committee be apprised of the developments in this regards.

INTERNATIONAL CO-OPERATION 
Recommendation  
6. The Committee appreciates the activities undertaken under the International Co-operation sub-
scheme particularly Youth 20 under G20 and Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Youth 
Conference. The Committee hopes that more such activities will take place in the year of G20 Presidency 
of India. The Committee observes that more students should be chosen from rural and far-flung areas of 
the country under International Co-operation for enhancing their exposure to global ideas, opportunities, 
values and best practices. 
(para 5.5) 
Action Taken 
The Ministry has stated that under International Cooperation Scheme of its Department of Youth 
Affairs, Indian Youth Delegates are nominated by this Department from diverse fields for which 
nominations are sought with the approval of competent authority from various reputed  universities/

balance including the youth from the rural and far flung areas. 
Comments of the Committee  
 The Committee takes note of the action taken by the Department in response to 
recommendation of the Committee. However, the Department has not given any details about the 
inclusion of youth be chosen from rural and far-flung areas of the country under International Co-
operation not it has provided the details about inclusion of youth from tier 2 and tier 3

YOUTH HOSTELS (YH)  
 
Recommendation  
7. On the basis of discussions held with the Department on the state of Youth Hostels, the 
Committee finds that the number of Youth Hostels need to be increased and provision of providing 
support staff should also be explored. The Committee is of the view that the Department should monitor 
quality standards, hygiene and infrastructure of Youth Hostels for meeting the ambitions of India's 
youth. 
(para 6.6) 

10 
 
 
Action Taken 
The Department has informed the Committee that the Department has sought more funds under 
YH Scheme for FY 2024-25 for making budget provisions under relevant head of the Youth Hostel 
Scheme for considerations of proposals that may be received from the State Governments  for 
construction of new Youth Hostels.  
 
It was also informed that regarding the provision of support staff, it is submitted that as per 
provisions contained in the Youth Hostel Manual, the appointment of Manager and Warden is done by 
the Central Government. The remaining staff is hired by Hostel Management Committee chaired by 
DC/ DM/ Secretary, D/o Youth Affairs (YA) of the concerned State, on need basis. Such staff is paid 
salary from the funds available in bank account of youth hostel. As regards maintaining quality 
standards of youth hostels, it is stated that as on date, 19 Youth Hostels are ISO:2015 certified. The 
Ministry is pursuing with remaining Youth Hostels as well to obtain ISO certification to maintain their 
quality standards. 
 
Comments of the Committee  
 
The Committee notes and appreciates the Ministry's attempts to secure ISO:2015 
certification for the Youth Hostels.  However, it would like to enquire about the delay in securing 
such certification for all hostels and any constraints the Ministry faces in this regard. It is also not 
evident that the certification alone will guarantee quality standards, hygiene and infrastructure for 
the hostels as envisioned by the Committee.  For instance, hostels should be equipped with Wi-Fi 
connectivity, secure locks, CCTV cameras, and round-the-clock security-all of which may fall 
outside the domain of such certification.  Moreover, the Departments should ensure a mechanism in 
place to seek feedback from hostellers and implement corrective action based on it.  
 
Recommendation  
8. The Committee observes that there is acute shortage of Youth Hostels for girls in the country. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Youth Affairs should construct Youth 
Hostels exclusively for girls in every capital city of each State. Further Youth Hostels for girls should 
also be constructed at places of educational centres, tourist destinations and places of historical and 
cultural value to facilitate them. 
(para 6.7) 
 
Action Taken 
The Department has informed the Committee that the Youth Hostels cater to accommodation 
for both boys and girls in Youth hostels and separate dormitories are there for boys and girls. The 
Ministry appoints Manager and his lady kin as warden to look after the needs of both boys and girls 
staying in the Youth Hostels. As per provisions of the Youth Hostel Manual, hostels are constructed at 
places of educational centres, tourist destinations and historical and cultural value. 
 
It was also informed that a Youth Hostel at Kota, Rajasthan is currently under construction. 
More funds have been sought under Budget Estimates 2024-25 under the youth hostel scheme for 
keeping a provision for construction of more Youth hostels. Proposals for construction of more Youth 
hostels will be considered by the Ministry upon receipt of proposals from the State Governments 
subject to viability of proposals, availability of funds and the approval of the component authority. 
 

11 
 
Comments of the Committee  
 
The Committee had recommended for construction of Youth Hostels for girls exclusively in 
the Capital cities of all the States/UTs in view of difficulties being faced by them. However, it is 
observed that the Department is silent in its Action Taken Note (ATN) in this regard. Further, only 
one Youth Hostel, at Kota is currently under construction. At this pace, the Committee apprehends 
that the Department may not be able to achieve the target of construction of Youth Hostels for girls 
exclusively to facilitate them in every capital city of States/UTs, places of educational centres, 
tourist destinations and places of historical and cultural values. 
 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should seek additional funds in 
Union Budget 2025-26 and ensure construction of Youth Hostels exclusively for girls in capital city 
of each State/UT, places of educational centres, tourist destinations and places of historical and 
cultural values to facilitate the girl students of the country, as recommended earlier by the 
Committee. The Committee may be apprised of the developments taking place in this regard.

22 
 
the hostels as envisioned by the Committee.  For instance, hostels should be equipped with Wi-Fi 
connectivity, secure locks, CCTV cameras, and round-the-clock security-all of which may fall 
outside the domain of such certification.  Moreover, the Departments should ensure a mechanism in 
place to seek feedback from hostellers and implement corrective action based on it.  
(Para 6.6) 
8. The Committee had recommended for construction of Youth Hostels for girls 
exclusively in the Capital cities of all the States/UTs in view of difficulties being faced by them. 
However, it is observed that the Department is silent in its Action Taken Note (ATN) in this regard. 
Further, only one Youth Hostel, at Kota is currently under construction. At this pace, the 
Committee apprehends that the Department may not be able to achieve the target of construction of 
Youth Hostels for girls exclusively to facilitate them in every capital city of States/UTs, places of 
educational centres, tourist destinations and places of historical and cultural values. 
 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should seek additional funds in 
Union Budget 2025-26 and ensure construction of Youth Hostels exclusively for girls in capital city 
of each State/UT, places of educational centres, tourist destinations and places of historical and 
cultural values to facilitate the girl students of the country, as recommended earlier by the 
Committee. The Committee may be apprised of the developments taking place in this regard. 
                                                      
(Para 6.7) 
ASSISTANCE TO SCOUTING & GUIDING ORGANISATIONS  
 
9. The Committee notes the action taken by the Department of Youth Affairs and 
observes that no compliance report has been sent to the Committee with respect to the 
Recommendation of the Committee contained in 354th Report. The Committee further observes 
that although the Scout and Guide movement has a rich history, there is still a gap in awareness 
about the benefits of participation in Scouts and Guides programs, particularly in rural areas. 
Additionally, many schools do not have dedicated Scout and Guide units, which limits the outreach 
of these programs.  
 The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department of Youth Affairs and Sports to 
engage school children with gender sensitization, environment protection initiatives, skill 
development, digital literacy and awareness about various schemes and programmes of the 
Government and furnish the compliance report in this regard to the Committee at the earliest.

Notes furnished by the Ministry. However, the Committee is of the view that correct reply/ figure 
with due diligence and after proper vetting by the authority concerned should be furnished for its 
consideration.

NEW INITIATIVES  
 
  
 
 11. The Committee notes that the Department of Youth Affairs has noted the 
recommendation of the Committee for compliance. However, Department has not furnished any

    REPORT 
 
The Report of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Education, Women, 
Children, Youth and Sports deals with the action taken by the Government on the 
Recommendations/Observations contained in its 3 41st Report on “ Review of  Education Standards, 
Accreditation Process, Research, Examination Reforms and Academic Environment in Deemed/ Private 
Universities/other Higher Education Institutions”, which was presented to the Rajya Sabha and laid on the 
Table of Lok Sabha on 04th July, 2022. 
 
2. The Action Taken Notes in respect of Recommendations/Observations contained in above 
mentioned Report were received from the Department of Higher Education, Ministry of Education vide 
their communication dated 18th April, 2024. These have been categorized as follows:  
 
Chapter I: Recommendations which have been accepted by the Government  
Paras –14, 20, 22, 26  
Total - 04 
 
Chapter II: Recommendations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of Government's 
replies:-

by the Committee:-

2 
 
CHAPTER-I 
RECOMMENDATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT 
 
Recommendation  
1. The Committee recommends for a deep study on improving educational standards through 
innovation in education, especially through the use of technology and based on such a study, a blueprint 
be prepared for each of the HEIs to be followed to enhance the sta ndards of education all across  the 
country. 
(Para 14) 
Action Taken 
 
Establishing and Functioning of Institution’s Innovation Councils (IICs) network in HEIs: 
 
The Department has informed that AICTE and MoE’s Innovation Cell have designed and are 
implementing a unique and first of its kind model called Institution’s Innovation Council (IIC) as an 
approach to institutionalizing innovation and startup culture in HEIs and further to create, streamline and 
strengthen existing ecosystems in HEIs. In jus t 5 years, a vibrant network of Institution's Innovation 
Councils (IICs) in more than 9000+ HEIs have spread across all 36 states and UTs. The IIC structure 
contributes to increasing awareness, encouraging and engaging academia in sustained generation of 
innovations and start-ups from academic institutions. 
A systematic functioning of an IIC in the campus ensures streamlining and strengthening the campus 
ecosystem by following measures: 
• Improving Institutions' Capability and Capacity of faculty in HEIs by  training and deployment as 
Innovation Ambassadors (IA) as on -ground change agent to drive and support innovation and 
entrepreneurship activities. 
• Promoting inter -institutional coordination and knowledge sharing through the Mentor -Mentee 
Program designed for IIC Institutions. 
• Empowering institutions from rural and aspirational districts of the country to get connected with 
regional startup ecosystems through the Impact Lecture (IL) Scries Program designed for IIC 
Institutions. 
• Enabling IIC institution s to build a strong pipeline of inventions, innovations and start -ups from 
HEIs and connecting with pre -incubation, incubation and ecosystem enablers for transformation 
into start-ups. 
• Providing mentoring and funding/grant support to Innovations through YUKTI Innovation 
Challenge (YIC), access to investors and incubation linkages. 
• Bridging higher education with schools through the Mentoring Linkage Support from Institutions' 
Innovation Council (IlCs) in HEIs with Atal Tinkering Labs (ATLs) and School In novation 
Councils (SICs) in Schools: 
• Enabling HEIs for adoption of the model course curriculum on innovation and entrepreneurship at 
School, UG and PG level 
• Imbibing an IP driven culture, facilitating IF5 commercialization and technology transfer throu gh 
the INDOVATION Centres setup in various regions of the country. 
• Ensuring and incentivizing HEIs for the IP literary through the implementation of KAPILA 
scheme to support IP filing in HEIs. 
• Providing hand holding support to HEIs in formulating institution's specifics Innovation and 
Startup Policy through the adoption of National Innovation and Startup Policy (NFSP) guidelines 
in HEIs. 

3 
 
• Providing knowledge sharing platform to IIC institutions and celebrating innovation culture by 
organizing Innovative Bharat IIC Regional Meets in different cities across the country on regular 
basis. 
• Facilitating institutions to take part in the Innovation Ranking Framework to Benchmarking I&E 
Ecosystem in HEIs and Schools. 
• Enabling IIC institutions to org anise internal hackathons and connect with National and 
International Hackathons for creative problem solving by putting them in Design Boot -Camps for 
Innovators, conducting Smart India Hackathon and Toycathon and scries of international 
hackathons for stu dents from HEIs and Schools to engage them in creative problem solving and 
startup development. 
 
• IIITs have been designed to impart education in the broad areas of Information Technology. A 
multidisciplinary approach is being implemented in these institu tions. Furthermore, 
recommendations will also be communicated to IITs for necessary action 
 
• The National Education Alliance of Technologies (NEAT) was introduced by AICTE/ MoE to 
verify, aggregate, and deliver EdTech solutions directly to the students, g iving them wide choice 
to select the technological solution that would suit their requirements, thereby improving their 
overall learning. 
 
AICTE is acting as a facilitator to ensure that the solutions are available to socially and 
economically weaker secti on students. AICTE would own and distribute 25 % free coupons from the 
registration of NEAT Portal for learning to the socially/economically weaker section of students as per the 
scheme. ICT therefore, could be adopted at the system level to enhance studen t learning engagement and 
outcomes, including their capacity to learn for life. 
 
 
 
Recommendation  
2. The Committee recommends that the Department of Higher Education should formulate policies/ 
initiatives keeping in view the Master Plans that States formulate towards the higher education sector. 
This will help, on the one hand in better resource allocation and coordination between the States and the 
Ministry in extending financial support, and on the other curb the tendency of politicization of approv als 
for colleges by Universities and State Governments. 
(Para 20) 
Action Taken 
 The Department has informed the Committee that the University Grants Commission as a policy, 
regularly consults all State Universities in matters pertaining to higher education. Further, a Committee 
constituted by AICTE under the Chairmanship of Shri BVR Mohan Reddy, Chairman, Board of 
Governors, IIT Hyder abad prepared short term and medium term perspective plan for engineering 
education wherein suggestions for introduction of courses in new emerging areas,  optimum utilization of 
existing intake capacity, teachers training etc. have been given. The Committee studied the current state of 
engineering education in India. It has analyzed AICTE data on intake capacity at UG and PG Level in 
engineering and enrolment trends across the country, several analyst and associations’ reports on the 
technologies, jobs and skills, and engineering education trends of the future. The recommendation of the 
committee has been implemented by AICTE and major policy decisions have been taken to put 

4 
 
moratorium on opening of new engineering institutions in traditional disciplines upto academic  year 
2023-24 with certain exceptions. 
 
Recommendation  
3. The Committee recommends that the Government give an active con sideration to the demand that 
deemed universities be allowed to use the term 'university' by amending Clause 23 of the UGC Act, 1956 
which states that no institution, other than a university established or incorporated by a Central Act, a 
Provincial Act or  a State Act is entitled to use the word 'University', as the term 'deemed university' 
creates a lot of confusion in foreign countries as there is no concept of deemed university in many parts of 
the world. 
(Para 22) 
 
Action Taken 
 The Committee is informed that NEP 2020 envisages University, worldwide, means a 
multidisciplinary institution of higher learning that offers undergraduate, graduate, and Ph.D. 
programmes, and engages in high -quality teaching and research. The present comp lex nomenclature of 
HEIs in the country such as ‘deemed to be  university’ , ‘affiliating university’ , ‘affiliating technical 
university’, ‘unitary university’ shall be replaced simply by ‘university’ on fulfilling the criteria as per 
norms.  
 
Recommendation  
4. The Committee recommends that the Department advise the HEIs to consider a ‘Unipass’ system 
like in many educational institutions abroad which comprises a digitally enabled card for utilization of all 
internal and external facilities pro vided by the HEIs and government to students. This is especially 
important given that most HEIs in India issue multiple paper cards like health card, library card etc. 
seParately to students. 
(Para 26) 
 
Action Taken 
 The Department has informed the Committee that UGC has taken note of this very important 
recommendation. A policy decision is required to be taken in consultation with the HEIs.   
 
 AICTE welcomes the suggestion given by the Committee and will explore the feasibility of 
introduction of Unipass (Digitally Enabled Card) in AICTE Approved Institutions in place  of 
multiple cards such as Identity Card, Library Card and Health Card etc. 
 Some IIMs provide their students with only one identity card which is RFID enabled and facilities 
multiple functions such as library access, hall ticket for examinations, entry -exit pass, interlinked 
with a biometric system that can track attendance and assist the academic departments to sort details 
in real-time. 
 Some are in process of integrating several internal and external facilities in Unipass system. 
 
 
 
 
 

5 
 
CHAPTER-II 
RECOMMENDATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE IN 
VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT'S REPLY 
Recommendation  
1. The Committee taking note of the thrust areas and the proposed reforms as outlined for the Higher 
education sector in the National Education Policy (NEP) - 2020 recommends that the Department of 
Higher Education must formulate a visionary blueprint with a clear time bou nd roadmap and strict 
monitoring mechanism, towards each of the policy directions for their successful, effective and time -
bound implementation. 
(Para 1) 
Action Taken 
The Department has submitted that NEP 2020 provides different timelines as well as principles 
and methodology for its implementation. After announcement of National Education Policy 2020, a 
number of consultations / deliberations have been held with stakeh olders for implementation of the 
National Education Policy 2020. Further, actionable activities of National Education Policy 2020 were 
identified/ prepared for the year 2020 -21 and 2021 -2022 and circulated among stakeholders for 
implementation.  
It was also informed that based on the deliberations / consultations with States/UTs  Government, 
18-points action plan capturing the quantifiable targets related to activities of N EP, 2020 has been 
prepared and shared with States/UTs for implementation during the Academic Year 2022-23. Further, a 3-
day National level Conference with Chief Secretaries of States was held on Implementation of NEP, 2020 
and implementation of NEP 2020 was also the agenda item of 7th meeting of the Governing Council of 
NITI Aayog held on 7 th August, 2022. To discuss and deliberate implementation of NEP, 2020 and

Recommendation  
1. The Committee notes that the National Education Policy, 2020 envisages the creation of the 
Higher Education Commission of India (HECI) as the principal regulator for higher education, with four 
verticals for regulation, accreditation, fu nding, and academic standards and also a Bill to provide for 
HECI is under drafting stage. The Committee, in this regard, recommends that the aspects relating to 
protection of interests of stakeholders, clear demarcation of its jurisdiction to avoid any re gulatory 
overlaps and gaps, independent nature with adequacy of resources and performance accountability be 
given due consideration. The Committee recommends that instead of having too many Parallel regulatory 
bodies in the higher education sector, a simpl ified hierarchy of regulatory bodies may be constituted 
which will have a final say in implementation of Government rules/regulations/acts etc. 
(Para 2) 
Action Taken 
 
 The Committee was informed that the  Government announced the NEP, 2020 on 29.07.2020. 
Regarding the regulatory system of higher education, the NEP, 2020 states that regulation of higher 
education has been too heavy -handed for decades; too much has been attempted to be regulated with too 
little effect. The mechanistic and disempowering nature of the regulatory system has been rife with very 
basic problems, such as heavy concentrations of power within a few bodies, conflicts of interest among 
these bodies, and a resulting lack of accountabilit y. The regulatory system is in need of a complete 
overhaul in order to re -energize the higher education sector and enable it to thrive. To address these 
issues, the NEP envisions setting up of a Higher Education Commission of India. In the backdrop of the 
NEP, 2020, for the implementation of the envisioned Regulatory System of Higher Education, the 
Department of Higher Education has prepared a draft Higher Education Commission of India Bill. The 
matter is being considered by Ministry of Education (MOE) in consultation with stakeholders. 
 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee observes that the multiplicity of regulators leads to inconsistency in 
standards and monitoring, making it difficult for institutions to function effectively. Moreover, 
State Universities, which educate over 90 per cent of the student population, are caught in between 
national and state -level regulations. The draft Higher Education Commission of India Bill (HECI) 
(which seeks to replace UGC as a single regulator) appears to perpetuate many of these same issues 
by maintaining a Central Government - heavy composition and insufficient State representation. 
The proposed HECI Bill will hold significant power, including the ability to grant degree -awarding 
authority and close institutions failing to meet standards. This removes State control and could lead 
to the closure of institutions in rural areas that suffer from infrastructure or faculty shortages. It 
would indirectly fuel privatization especially in rural areas . The Committee, therefore,  
recommends that a simplified hierarchy of regulatory bodies would be more effective, the 
Department should ensure that any such unified regulatory body must have adequate 
representation for all States and there should not be excess centralization.
