leadership qualities in women youth.  The example of women leaders of the past should be 
used to inspire the younger generations through the NYLP, as well as through the 
activities of the NSS and NYKS. 
(Para 2.7.6) 
24. The Committee notes that the Department has been using the MY Bharat portal to create 
awareness about Government schemes and to engage youth in a dialogue on public policy. 
The Department has hosted a series of programs such as the Viksit Bharat YuvaConnect 
program, aimed at fostering youth engagement and leadership in the developmental 
transformation of India, in many educational institutions across the country since its 
launch in Pune in September 16, 2024. In the Viksit Bharat Young Leaders Dialogue final 
stage, over 2,400 youth participated in an interaction with hon'ble Prime Minister himself. 
The Department has also conducted activities like “Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam” and 
interactions with ministers and eminent speakers from the field of sports and 
entrepreneurship. The Committee notes that the biggest challenge faced by the 
Department however is that of creating awareness of its schemes, including MY Bharat. 
(Para 2.8.9) 
25. The Committee notes that the performances and the achievements of the Nehru Yuva 
Kendra and all programme conducted by the DoYA under different schemes are reported 
on the My Bharat portal. The Committee noted that according to the figures for FY 2024-
25 provided above, the expenditure as on 31.01.25 under the Scheme stood only at Rs. 7.50 
Crores, which is a gross underutilisation of funds.  The Committee was informed that the 
utilization of the fund was for establishing Mera Yuva Bharat (MY Bharat) as an 
autonomous body.  The reason provided that decrease of expenditure is due to trend, does 
not suffice.  The Committee observes that the Budget for the FY 2025-26 has been 
decreased. The Committee would like to know as to how this cut would affect the 
functioning of the Scheme. 
(Para 2.8.10) 
26. The Committee notes that the vacancies of NSS volunteers are around 50%.  Hence, there 
is an urgent need to fill these vacancies especially in colleges and universities. The 

65 
 
Department should develop an action plan to fill the same and share it with the 
Committee.  
(Para 2.9.8) 
27. The Committee notes that various states have taken initiative to reward and recognize the 
contributions of NSS volunteers, but that there is a wide variation in the policy adopted by 
different states. The Committee recommends the Department try to bridge this gap by 
developing and radiating a common framework for the same. In particular, the 
Committee recommends that the Department of Youth Affairs work with the Department 
of Higher Education to ensure that service hours undertaken by NSS volunteers are 
creditized in the Academic Bank of Credits accepted by HEIs.  
(Para 2.9.9) 
28. The Committee notes the proposal to transform the NSS into the National Service and 
Skill Development Scheme. It recommends that the transition should be expedited. It 
further recommends that the NSS take up communal harmony and drug abstention and 
de-addiction as major thrusts for its activities going forward. Like with the NYKS, the 
Committee recommends that all youth programs must begin with oath taking of the 
Preamble to the Constitution, and the recitation of the National Pledge. 
(Para 2.9.10) 
29. The Committee recommends that there should be a regular impact assessment of 
volunteer schemes to track the tangible contributions made by volunteers under this 
scheme and understand how these programs can be improved in future years 
(Para 2.9.11) 
30. The Committee observed that for the FY 2024-25 the utilization of funds as on 31.01.25 is 
just Rs. 16 Crores while the RE for the year was Rs. 23.50 crores.  This is a notable under 
utilisation of funds.  However, the reason quoted while seeking the funds for BE 2025-26 
are disbursement of salaries and recruitment of Teaching and non-teaching staff. The 
Committee notes that the RGNIYD has been entrusted with the responsibility for training, 
documentation, research and evaluation and extension for all youth related activities in 
the country.  The Institute should be more pro-active in its utilisation of funds to deliver 
on its mission.  
(Para 2.10.14) 
31. The Committee was informed that all 5 positions for Professor in RGNIYD are currently 
vacant. The Committee was further informed that previous attempts to fill these positions 
were unsuccessful since no suitable applications were received. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry should look into the reasons for the same and take suitable 
corrective action if required, including possibly revisiting existing compensation, and 
working more closely with Universities for a wider dissemination of job advertisements. 
(Para 2.10.15) 
32. The Committee appreciates the Schemes which provide incentives and special cash awards 
to the sportspersons in recognition of their talents and the laurels they bought to the 
country, including the National Sports Awards, Cash Incentives, post-retirement pension 
etc.  The Govt. of India also provides a quota to sportspersons in jobs (upto 5%). Besides 
this, for Welfare, scheme for financial assistance to sportspersons with poor financial 

66 
 
condition is also operative.  The Committee however recommends that more be done to 
recognize our sportspersons. The prize money sportspersons win in prestigious 
competitions may be declared tax-exempt. 
(Para 5.1.5) 
33. The Committee notes that the Department of Sports is making an effort to provide 
financial assistance not only at the institutional level but also at the individual level.  It 
appreciated the efforts that the investments are not in all category of events / sports for 
sending the teams abroad for training, participating in international events, conducting 
international events in India, national championship events and for procuring sports 
equipment. Financial assistance is also extended through SAI for organizing coaching 
camps, for preparing national teams and for engaging the services of foreign coaches but 
also to provide comprehensive support to athletes with disabilities, covering aspects like 
training, competition exposure, medical support, travel, and financial assistance to ensure 
that India’s athletes are well-prepared for major events like the Paralympics Games, 
World Championships, and other international competitions.  The Committee 
recommends that the Department continue its initiatives and provide further resources to 
athletes and institutions under this scheme. 
(Para 5.3.10) 
34. The Committee recommends that the Department should integrate their strategy for 
talent hunt in all the games and sports with the National Sports Policy and that it should 
be synergized with the games at the school, district, state and national level. It should be 
continuous and ongoing process on yearly basis at all levels, so that sports talent is 
adequately identified and recognized. The Committee notes that it is heartening that SAI 
has deputed High Performance Analyst (HPA) Nutritionist at each NCOE to take care of 
the dieting and nutrition requirement of athletes. However, itrecommended that the 
Department give additional focus to the nutritional components of sports persons training 
in the SAI Training Centers (STCs), Extension Centers of STCs, and National Sports 
Talent Contest centers as well. The Committee recommended that places like Haryana, 
Manipur, Punjab, etc. which are famous for particular sports, need to be invested in to 
further develop the sports ecosystem in these states.  
(Para 5.3.11) 
35. The Committee recommends that education and sports need to be synchronized.  Special 
schools need to be established to promote such talents without compromising on school / 
college education.  The Committee noted that successful examples of sports education in 
foreign countries should be studied for adaptation in India as well.  Sport integrated 
learning, as envisioned in the NEP, should be promoted.  The collaboration of SAI, private 
players, the Ministry of Education, and State Governments should be materialized 
through a policy and at the ground level a sports-school curricula should be evolved.  The 
National Code for Good Governance in Sports should be paradigm for formulating the 
above policy, including CSR funds from some international brands and curricula.  This 
would bring about transparency and accountability in this field. 
(Para 5.3.12)  
36. The Committee noted that while the budget of Department of Sports has increased 
substantially in the last ten years, there is a need to further augment the financial 
resources for sports.  The Committee recommends that the Department attempt to 
maximize utilization of the budget to seek greater allocations in the coming years.  

67 
 
(Para 5.3.13) 
37. The Committee recommends that young sportspersons should be supported in their 
academic journeys so as to not have to be forced to choose between the two. Accordingly, 
the Committee recommends that all NCOEs and SAI regional centers establish residential 
sports schools with curriculum and school structure developed to specifically support 
sportspersons. 
(Para 5.3.14) 
38. The Committee notes that funds are allocated Scheme-wise and not State-wise in this 
Ministry. The Khelo India Scheme is a demand-driven scheme. The proposals received 
from the State/UT Governments and other eligible entities are considered for financial 
support, subject to their completeness, technical feasibility and availability of funds under 
the Scheme in line with the twin objectives of mass participation and promotion of 
excellence in sports to infuse sports culture in the country. Further the Detailed Project 
Reports (DPRs) received from the States are meticulously studied and the States are 
guided in respect of the shortcoming.  Hence, the Committee recommends that the 
Department should constantly monitor the utilization certificates and completion 
certificates. The Committee noted that so far, a total of 321 projects worth Rs 3080 Crores 
have been sanctioned under Khelo India Scheme, of which over 200 are complete.  
(Para 5.4.9) 
39. The Committee notes that budget utilization in Khelo India needs to be improved and that 
it was only ~60% in FY23 and 87.2% in FY24. The Committee recommends the 
Department work more closely with State Governments to achieve the same. Further, 
specific provisions must be made to support the promotion and development of Hockey. 
(Para 5.4.10) 
40. The Committee noted that the development of sports in the Northeast must be given 
special attention and focus. Due to the higher costs faced in this region, additional funds 
should be made available to NCOEs in this region, in collaboration with Ministry for 
DoNER and other agencies. 
(Para 5.4.11) 
41. The Committee noted that the Khelo India Games being organized by theDepartment of 
Sports are enabling talented young sportspersons to get experience of international 
standard events. A total of 16 editions of these Games have been hosted so far, where more 
than 50,000 athletes have participated, transforming the sports competition landscape in 
India. The Committee recommends that the Khelo India Games be held annually so as to 
ensure maximum participation of sportspersons in these games. The Committee further 
recommends that the name and eligibility of the Khelo India University games may be 
shifted solely to the age of the participant, to ensure a level playing field for all 
sportspersons who any not be enrolled in HEIs.  
(Para 5.4.12) 
42. The Committee recommends that the disbursement of funds under Khelo India be 
directed towards investment in sportspersons, coaching, nutrition and health support, and 
investments in field-of-play over large-scale infrastructure projects like stadiums. 
(Para 5.4.13) 
43. The Committee understood that enhanced infrastructure for J&K is provided to create 
better prospects for sportspersons. The Committee recommends that in J&K, the 

68 
 
improvement of sports infrastructure and the regular happening of sports events in 
Jammu and Kashmir has made it an emerging hub of sports. Be it cricket, martial arts, 
volleyball, athletics and other sports, regular competitions are being organised in the 
Union Territory under the ‘Khelo India’ programme. This has encouraged many players 
to qualify for national and international sports events. Hence, the organization of Sports 
events and activities is being promoted as a economic and cultural activity also.  
(Para 5.5.2) 
44. After going through the financial data submitted by the Ministry, the Committee observed 
that under the scheme of SAI there is an increase in need for funds due to establishment 
expenditure and to balance out to the expenditure, the amount was adjusted from the 
internal revenue. It recommends that the funds allocated should be expended only within 
its limits. The Committee hopes that proper procedure followed for adjusting the amount 
within the allocated budget of the Ministry. It was surprised to learn that in spite of SAIs’ 
demand for rising expenditure, only Rs. 830.00 crores was allocated in the BE 2025-26. 
The Committee would like to direct the Department of Sports to justify its expenditure vis-
à-vis BE 2025-26. 
(Para 5.6.17) 
45. The Committee observed from the data given above, that the recruitment situation in SAI 
is really needs attention. The staff position in Administrative cadre, Rajbhasha, Engineers 
& Sports Science (regular) Group A and B, Coaching Cadre, contractual personnel need 
to be filled up as urgently as possible. The Committee notes that such vacancies inevitably 
compromise the functioning of the institution.  
(Para 5.6.18) 
46. The Committee notes that another major issue that really hurts young sportspersons is 
that of over-age children competing in lower age groups. The Committee recommends that 
the Department consider solutions to this issue.  
(Para 5.6.19) 
47. The Committee recommended that all SAI regional centers must have adequate hostel 
capacity to provide residential facilities for all sportspersons. The Department is 
recommended to provide funds for the same. 
(Para 5.6.20) 
48. The Committee was informed that “As per the Recruitment Rules for the Coaching 
Cadre, a total of 1,524 posts have been sanctioned across all positions within the Coaching 
Cadre, including HPC, Coach, Senior Coach, Assistant Coach, and Chief Coach. Out of 
these 1,524 sanctioned posts, 685 are designated for contractual or deputation 
engagement. However, against these 685 posts, 307 coaches were working in the FY2024.” 
The Committee recommends that this trend of contractualising coaching positions must be 
halted.  
(Para 5.6.21) 
49. The Committee notes that the current sports talent scouting infrastructure for the country 
includes the 67 STCs (SAI Training Centers), 26 STC Extension Centers, and 68 NSTC 
(National Sports Talent Contest) centers across the country. The Committee recommends 
that this infrastructure be expanded over time with the goal of at least one talent scouting 
center in each district of the country, with the goal of scouting for sports talent between 
the age of 8 years and 14 years. The talent so scouted should be supported through 

69 
 
enrolment in the NCOEs, where the amenities extended to them should be expanded to 
eventually provide sports training cum residential facilities cum schooling. The 
sportspersons at NCOEs should have the facility for education cum sports training, along 
with the best of the coaching facilities, nutrition support, sports medicine, and mental 
counselling as part of the training program. The screening should be dynamic, and 
sportspersons must be held to high standards to retain their spot in the NCOEs. 
(Para 5.6.22) 
50. The Committee notes that a number of excellent sports persons are left out in villages and 
other remote areas who can excel in sports because they don't have adequate resources to 
pursue their games. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department of Sports 
and SAI to conduct rallies along the lines of recruitment rallies of Army to identify such 
sportspersons in their early ages and to groom them with adequate training and financial 
aid. This will help the country to excel other countries in field of sports. 
(Para 5.6.23) 
51. The Committee recommends that the increase in allocation of funds should be spent on 
strengthening the organization by appointing new manpower in all the categories of posts 
like Groups A, B and C and in providing proper representation of all classes of the society.  
(Para 5.7.8) 
51. The Committee notes the numerous programs undertaken through the Fit India 
Movement, as part of Khelo India. The Committee also notes that the ASMITA 
initiative launched under the Khelo India scheme has made an impact in promoting 
women participation in sports across India. The Committee appreciates the initiative 
which covers 20 disciplines now and recommends that the Department further enhance 
the initiative.  The Committee recommends that the Department continue to focus its 
efforts on inclusion, i.e., organize programs for women, persons with disabilities, and 
other underrepresented groups.  
(Para 5.8.2) 
52. The Committee notes that the Department of Sports has prioritized promotion of para-
sports in all spheres through cash incentives, National Sports Awards, dedicated 
training facilities, and support under TOPS scheme. This has resulted in historic wins 
in international events, including 29 medals in the Paris 2024 Paralympics. The 
Committee appreciates the same.  
(Para 5.8.3) 
53. The Committee notes that India ranks second in doping in the world, which is an 
unfortunate development. However, the Committee appreciates that the crucial role 
played by NADA in guiding and regulating sportspersons to ensure fair play, integrity 
and adherence to anti-doping rules. The Committee notes that the shortage of staff in 
the Department of Sports and the NADA may impact its performance.  Therefore, the 
Committee recommends that the vacant positions in all categories of posts should 
immediately be filled in. 
(Para 5.10.18) 
54. The Committee notes and appreciates that the Department and NADA have 
successfully expanded the scale of dope testing by 75% in recent years, from 4,260 tests 
in 2022 to 7.466 tests in 2024 
(Para 5.10.19)  

70 
 
55. The Committee noted that the National Sports University offers a Masters in Physical 
Education course for the duration of two years, with the capacity of thirty seats. There 
is also a Bachelors in Physical Education with fifty seats, and a Master of Science in 
Sports & Coaching course with twenty seats. The Committee recommends that the 
number of seats available under these programs be increased. The Committee also 
recommends that the University be accompanied by a sports school to provide 
educational and residential facilities to sportspersons below the age of 18 years. 
Further, the Committee appreciates the progress in the completion of building NSU’s 
permanent campus in spite of the current disturbances in the state of Manipur. 
(Para 5.11.13) 
56.  The Committee notes that the National Sports University in Manipur is the only 
institution of its kind in the country and was established by an Act of Parliament in 2018. 
It has been running from a temporary facility at Khuman Lampak in Imphal while 
construction activities for the permanent campus at Koutruk are ongoing. The Committee 
notes that the University does not currently have a regular Vice-Chancellor or the 
required faculty. The Committee recommends that the construction of the campus be 
expedited, and that a permanent, full-time Vice Chancellor be appointed so that the 
recruitment of required faculty members may also occur. 
(Para 5.11.14) 
57. The Committee notes that the Department has provisioned for post-retirement support for 
ex-sportspersons who have brought laurels to the country, and that over 850 sportspersons 
have been awarded lifelong pension ranging up to Rs. 20,000/- per month. The Committee 
observes that the career of sports persons and their pensions should be made lucrative so 
that the required talent is attracted and retained properly. Accordingly, the Committee 
recommends that the pension due to meritorious sportspersons be not less than the 
pension accorded to a retired Class 1 Officer. 
(Para 5.12.1) 
58. The Committee recommends that the Department take proactive steps to train high 
quality coaches within the country. Furthermore, the Committee recommends that the 
Department institute a protocol that medical professionals should compulsorily 
accompany sports persons in all Games overseas. 
(Para 5.15.1) 
59. The Committee notes that the National Games are typically organized by the Indian 
Olympic Association (IOA) biennially, but that they weren’t organized between 2015 
and 2022, partly due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The Committee recommends that 
the Department work more closely with the Indian Olympic Association to ensure that 
the same is not repeated in the future. The Committee also recommends that the 
Department consider supporting the IOA in organizing the National Games annually. 
The Department may assist the IOA with identifying cities with the requisite sporting 
infrastructure and host the games there so as to avoid having to incur high expenses on 
capital expansion. 
(Para 5.16.1)

Children, Youth and Sports deals with the action taken by the Government on the 
Recommendations/Observations contained in its 358th Report of the Department-related Parliamentary 
Standing Committee (DRPSC) on Education, Women, Children, Youth and Sports on ‘Research based

Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on 13th December, 2023.

mentioned Report were received from the Department of Higher Education, Ministry of Education vide

CHAPTER-I 
RECOMMENDATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT 
 
Recommendation  
1. The Committee has observed the contamination of arsenic, fluoride and the presence of other 
heavy metals in ground and drinking water across multiple states. This contamination is contributing to 
severe health issues such as cancer, skin diseases, cardiovascular disease, and diabetes among the 
inhabitants in affected regions and States. Additionally, the Committee notes that substantial research 
dedicated to eradicating arsenic, fluoride, and other heavy metals from ground and drinking water in these 
affected areas is urgently needed to address the issue. Taking note of the magnitude of the issue, the 
Committee strongly recommends that the Department of Science and Technology, Department of Health 
Research, and Department of Higher Education, including various esteemed institutions like IITs should 
prioritize and fund comprehensive research initiatives aimed at eliminating arsenic, fluoride, and other 
heavy metals detrimental to health from ground and drinking water within the affected regions and states 
upon a mapping of such territories. This proactive step will not only address the immediate health hazards 
but also pave the way for sustainable, innovative solutions towards effective waste water management 
and saline water treatment practices. 
(Para 6.4 of the 358th Report of the Committee) 
Action Taken 
Department of Higher Education 
I.  Noted. UGC has been advising HEIs from time to time regarding sustainability practices. UGC 
has brought out the Guidelines on Institutional Development Plan (IDP). The IDP aims to guide Higher 
Education Institutions to chalk developmental plans that are specific to their institution.  The plan 
identifies various interconnected enabler parameters representing a vertical to reflect an integrated 
approach including the ‘Research, and Intellectual Property Enablers’ and ‘Networking and Collaborating 
Enablers' as parameters for excellence.  The guidelines provide guidance to HEIs to achieve excellence in 
their identified areas. Further, these lay down a framework for steering the HEIs towards self-
sustainability. 
II.  The recommendations of the committee have been noted. Necessary instructions have been issued 
to IITs in this regard. 
III.  SPAs (School of Planning and Architecture) have taken up research in the fields of Architecture, 
Planning including Landscape Architecture, Environmental Planning etc. SPAs are working on protection 
of water bodies by undertaking extensive research. The Institutes have Landscape Architecture, 
Environmental planning departments etc. working in this line. 
Department of Science & Technology 
Water Technology Initiative (WTI) of DST is a demand oriented user centric initiative which 
promotes developmental research in laboratories as well as application led research in the field. WTI 

3 
 
works through periodic thematic calls. The program has supported and nurtured approximately 55 
national & bilateral Research Development and Deployment (RD&D) activities in the area of Arsenic, 
Flouride and heavy metals monitoring and remediation technologies for Applied Research, Technology 
Development & Assessment and for providing customized Convergent Solutions. Some of the successful 
interventions which resulted in technology development and deployment in real conditions are listed in 
Arsenic Compendium published and developed by DST (attached). 
This programme also promotes and facilitates entire technology chain from technology 
development to commercialization. Two Arsenic treatment and mitigation technologies developed and 
commercialized through DST’s intervention are listed below: 
1. Laterite based Arsenic filter which uses naturally abundant raw laterite modified by suitable 
chemical treatment. The technology requires no power for functioning. It removes Arsenic, Iron and 
Bacteriological contamination. The Technology has already been transferred to West Bengal based start 
up, IIT Kharagpur. 
2. AMRIT is an affordable solution for providing clean drinking water in arsenic affected areas. It is 
a gravity- fed water purification unit in which arsenic and iron containing water is passed through a 
composite filter unit to obtain water, conforming to international standards. The AMRIT Technology has 
already been transferred to a Chennai based start up through DST funded Business Incubator housed at 
IIT Madras. 
Department of Health Research  
Elimination of heavy metals from groundwater is not within the purview of ICMR. This may be 
taken up by DST. 
Department of Scientific & Industrial Research 
Department has noted the observation of the committee and submits that CSIR, an autonomous 
organization with Department of Scientific & Industrial Research, through its constituent laboratories is 
working for development of techno-economically feasible solutions for removal of arsenic, fluoride and 
other contaminants from ground/drinking water. Some of the technologies, namely Nalgonda and Solar 
Electrolytic Defluoridation Techniques for fluoride removal, Terafil and Ceramic filters for Arsenic and 
Iron removal, have been already deployed and several plants are running in the field. 
Further, CSIR is also funding/ executing various research projects for the effective addressing of this 
issue. Some of the CSIR research projects which are running/ successfully completed are given below:    
i. Comprehending aquifer Heterogeneities and hydrodynamics for Sustainable groundwater 
Management (CHASM); 
ii. Production of High-Quality Mineralized Water in Arid Regions using Indigenous Membrane 
Integrated Atmospheric Water Generator Systems Powered by Solar Energy; 
iii. Nanotechnology intervention for water purification and treatment;  
iv. Design and development of indigenous Membrane Distillation unit for treating RO reject (high 
saline water) and producing potable water;  

4 
 
v. Development of gravity operated domestic water filter for Removal of Arsenic from portable 
water under Indian Scenario;  
vi. Point of use (POU) filters for Arsenic Remediation in Drinking water; and   
vii. Design, development and optimization of cost effective advanced sensor for detection of 
contaminants (Arsenic and Fluoride) in different source of water 
In order to develop and scale-up, end-to-end solutions including sludge management for removal of 
fluoride, arsenic, iron and other geo-genic contaminants, CSIR is in process of consolidating the various 
water treatment technologies developed across CSIR constituent laboratories, at different TRL for the 
management of geo-genic contaminants in water, for the possible collaboration with different Central and 
State government agencies as well as with established corporates, to facilitate widespread application in 
the field for the benefit of the society. 
Recommendation  
2. The Committee appreciates the cutting-edge characterization and fabrication facilities, such as 
SATHI and Nano research facilities, within some Higher Education Institutions (HEIs). These facilities 
serve as central research hubs, open to researchers, students, and industry professionals nationwide. 
However, the operational expenses for these facilities, including Annual Maintenance Contracts (AMC), 
support technicians' salaries, and consumables, pose a significant financial burden. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends for having a structured support scheme specifically for catering to maintenance 
and operational costs. This scheme can operate on a model that accounts for the number of external users 
accessing these facilities. It is also felt that sustained accessibility to vital research infrastructure would 
get ensured, fostering a more equitable and enabling environment for cutting-edge research and 
innovation in the country by implementing such a scheme. 
(Para 6.11 of the 358th Report of the Committee) 
Action Taken 
Department of Higher Education 
SPAs (School of Planning and Architecture) are continuously improving research facilities. D/o 
Higher Education has duly noted the recommendation.

In pursuance of the above observations/recommendations by the Hon’ble Committee,

intensifying the base of S&T Infrastructure and human resources development, S&T led innovation and

Recommendation  
3. The Committee appreciates the concerted efforts by the Government, involving various 
Departments and agencies like the Department of Higher Education, Department of Science and 
Technology, Department of Scientific and Industrial Research, Department of Biotechnology, Department 
of Health Research/ICMR, Department of Agricultural Research/ICAR, and others in various areas of 
research and recommends for a coordinated, collaborative approach to actively foster private partnerships 
in scientific research and related fields. The Committee is of the view that strategic collaboration with 
private entities is essential to alleviate the burden on Government funding and ensure adequate financial 
support for research endeavours in science and allied disciplines. It is also felt that by proactively 
engaging in partnerships with the private sector, the Government can facilitate a more sustainable and 
diversified funding ecosystem for scientific research as these collaborative efforts will not only reduce the 
Government's financial burden but also it will harness the expertise and resources of the private sector to 
drive innovation and scientific advancement. Encouraging and nurturing such partnerships will create a 
conducive environment for ground-breaking research and will ensure a more balanced distribution of 
funding responsibilities between the public and private sectors. 
(Para 6.12 of the 358th Report of the Committee) 
Action Taken 
Department of Higher Education 
I.  UGC acknowledges the crucial need for strong connections between universities and industries to 
promote innovation, enhance employability, and drive economic growth. Accordingly, the UGC 
introduced the Guidelines on Sustainable and Vibrant University-Industry Linkage System for 
Indian Universities which aim to encourage collaboration between academia and industry, fostering a 
dynamic ecosystem for research, innovation, and knowledge transfer. 
Further, the UGC Guidelines on Institutional Development Plans for Higher Education Institutions 
(HEIs) encourage the establishment of Industry Relations Cell (IRC) at university/college level. While 
defining the responsibilities of the Industry Relations Cell (IRC), mention the following- 
a.  Liaisoning with local industry and enabling the realization of the proposed R&D culture involving 
own Universities/Institutes/Colleges and the industry.  

6 
 
b.  Identifying research topics of interest, including those that have local/regional relevance and 
dissemination of the same among the stakeholders.  
c.  Identification of potential problems for collaboration, creation of links between the concerned

e.  Explore sources of funding for the cell.  
f.  Drive the actions related to supporting student internships and apprenticeship with the help of the

II.  Activities such as Hackathon, Innovation challenges are organized by the Innovation Cell and

IV.  Policies like ISTEM can definitely provide impetus to Research, especially to individuals and

Department of Space 
1) Dhruva Space, Hyderabad, a pioneer among space startups in India developed a payload called 
LEAP-TD and was launched in PSLV C58 on 1st Jan 2024. It was accommodated in the POEM platform 
that was orbiting in a 350 km orbit. IIST’s ground station facility is jointly operated by IIST and Dhruva 
Space teams; the first beacon and telemetry from LEAP-TD was received on January 2nd and till date the 
payload is being tracked by the IIST ground station periodically. Telecommand from IIST ground station 
and reception of the telemetry from the payload are carried out periodically. 
2) With this IIST has entered into the domain of services for reliable ground station tracking systems 
and small satellites providing opportunities for universities and space startups to exploit these facilities on 
a mutually agreeable basis. In today's world of rapidly advancing space technologies and aligning with 
the country’s goal IIST has started collaborating with Universities and Industries in building small 
satellites and payloads using innovative technologies for miniaturizing systems, improving performance, 
reducing cost and rapid deployment of space assets in space. 
3) In the context of new space reforms, IIST has initiated measures to engage with private industries. 
An MOU signed with L&T is aimed at developing newer technologies associated with satellite and 
launch vehicle systems. One such fruitful engagement with L&T resulted in the launch of a 3D-printed 
pilot module payload in the 4th stage of PSLV in April 2023. 
4) Also, the technology transfer related to Atomic layer deposition with Quazer Tech Pvt Ltd. was 
successfully completed. In addition to the aforementioned areas, the institute is aggressively trying to 

7 
 
engage with more and more industries to jointly develop product and technology-oriented solutions for 
the industry and societal applications.

launched by PSLV C55. LI-SAT satellite is proposed to be launched in the first industrial PSLV.

Recommendation  
4. The Committee is of the view that research on India's traditional knowledge systems not only 
enriches the country's heritage but also offers viable solutions to contemporary challenges in healthcare, 
agriculture, and sustainability and this holistic approach towards development is imperative for India's 
progress and cultural preservation. In view of this, the Committee recommends prioritizing research in 
India's traditional knowledge systems due to their immense significance on multiple fronts such as Vedic 
mathematics, heritage preservation as it plays a pivotal role in preserving and documenting the ancient 
wisdom and practices inherent in traditional knowledge systems, validating the efficacy of traditional 
medical systems like Ayurveda and Yoga, sustainable practices in respect of agricultural methods, 
ecological wisdom, and natural resource management. 
(Para 6.15 of the 358th Report of the Committee) 
Action Taken 
Department of Higher Education 
I.  NEP 2020 envisages the promotion of Bharatiya Jnana Parampara (Indian Knowledge Systems). 
To facilitate a seamless integration of Bharatiya Paramparagat Jnana with modern stream, UGC has come 
up with ‘Guidelines for incorporation Indian Knowledge System (IKS) in Higher Education 
Curricula’. Further, UGC has also come up with ‘Guidelines for Training of Faculty on IKS’ for its 
integration in curriculum at all levels of education which will inspire the faculty in higher education 
institutions of the country to generate a positive attitude, explore and undertake quality research on IKS, 
and herald a new era in higher education ecosystem of the country in the light of NEP 2020. This 
guideline will also be a part of the training module under ‘Malaviya Mission’, and will be considered 
under CAS scheme as per the UGC regulations. 
In addition, Training in Bharatiya Jnana Parampara (Indian Knowledge Systems) is being 
undertaken. 
i. Six-days’ Basic Training Programme in Indian Knowledge Systems was organized at 06 
HRDCs/MMTTCs for above 1000 faculty from various HEIs across the country. The training 
program was based on three points: parampara (tradition), dristhi (perspective) and laukika 
prayojana (modern relevance) of Traditional Indian Knowledge Systems. 
ii. Further, among the faculty who underwent Six-days’ Basic Training Programme in Indian 
Knowledge Systems, through all India basis examination, 200 faculty are selected for Six-days’ 
Masters’ Training in IKS to meet the need of trained-faculty in IKS for training nearly 10,000 
faculty from HEIs across the country. The training is primarily aimed at the knowledge domains, 
sources, vocabulary, philosophical foundations and methods of IKS. 

9 
 
iii. In addition, finally for the Master Trainers’, a ‘Discipline Specific Training Programme’ based on 
the discourses and case studies in foundational aspects of Ayurveda, Mathematics, Arthashastra,

organized by UGC in collaboration with IKS Division of Ministry of Education, Govt. of India.

Department of Space 
Starting from the 2023-2024 academic year, IIST has introduced a new institute elective on Indian 
Knowledge Systems (IKS) for all its undergraduate students, a three-credit course designed to align with

values demonstrated by ancient Indian thinkers. It broadly covers the development of mathematics and 
astronomy, their applications in allied fields, the scientific principles underlying Indian musical 
instruments, and offers insights into human aspirations through the wisdom of ancient Indian thinkers. 
1) With the rollout of the new National Education Policy, India Knowledge Systems and Heritage 
(IKS&H) are becoming increasingly prominent in academic curricula. Consequently, several scholarly

10 
 
published by HTSR Institute, Bangalore. The book focuses on the fundamental principles to create a

2) Research based on Finite element analysis of the membrane is currently being carried out to

Department of Science & Technology 
In order to strengthen India's traditional knowledge systems, DST established a Dedicated Science 
and Heritage Research Initiative (SHRI) Cell in August 2022 to build capacity of human resource and 
encourage new researchers to work in the area of Heritage Science. DST is promoting R&D activities for 
preservation, conservation and propagation of tangible and intangible Heritage in India. DST has been 
supporting research projects on documentation and validation of traditional practices, material 
deterioration and restoration, new materials, preservation, diagnostic technologies, exploring new state-
of-art technologies to preserve heritage and artworks from ancient times, evolution and growth of human 
civilization, and promoting application of advanced knowledge of archaeometry science. 
The following four dedicated Centres for R&D on specialized areas have also been supported 
under SHRI Cell: 
•       "Takshashila Centre for Multidisciplinary Heritage Science" at IIT Hyderabad. The Centre has 
launched India’s first interdisciplinary Master's and Doctoral degree programs in Heritage Science and 
Technology to develop human resource in this niche area. Apart from generating human resource this 
Centre is also fostering innovative technologies like semi-automated OCR post-processing method to 
enhance text alignment, quality, and readability in complex document scenarios, including multi-language 
and multi-column texts. 
•      “Centre for Traditional, Complementary foods of Western Himalayas” at CSIR-IHBT Palampur” 
was established for documentation and characterization of traditional complementary foods from the 
Western Himalayan region and processing technologies. A compendium of 75 traditional recipes of 
Himachal Pradesh has already been published and this Centre is currently working on process 
standardization of traditional recipes of Himachal Pradesh. 
• “Centre for Conservation of Heritage Structures” at CSIR-CBRI, Roorkee - to conserve heritage 
structure and conducting research on several important aspects viz. non-destructive evaluation, material 
development, testing of heritage structure, data base development, health monitoring technologies, repair 
and restoration methodologies. 
•  “Indian Heritage in Digital Space- Immersive Digital Visualization of Ajanta, Ellora and 
Dwaraka” at Pravartak Technologies Foundation, IIT Madras. DST is further supporting scientific 
validation of yoga and meditation through its dedicated programme Science and Technology for Yoga 
and Meditation (SATYAM).

2. A community-based three arm multi-centric randomized controlled trial has been initiated to

11 
 
3. ICMR-NITM, Belagavi is currently undertaking scientific validation of selected non-codified

Department of Agriculture Research & Education (ICAR) 
ICAR is working on the traditional knowledge which encompasses the cultural traditions, values, 
beliefs, and understanding of local people in various aspects.  Studies revealed that the economic 
prosperity and sustainability of tribes across India basically depends on their traditional wisdom to 
manage land and crop resources and farming practices. Among these, land use, biodiversity, conservation 
tillage, organic waste recycling, green leaf manuring from live fences and growing leguminous cover 
crops in plantations are very important tribal practices. Scientific evaluation of these indigenous soil and 
crop management techniques maintains the soil fertility without much degradation of soil and sustains the 
agricultural productivity and its diversity.

groundwater.  In addition, split application and placement of fertilizers, use of slow releasing N-fertilizers

approach through formulation of a blueprint to bolster the research scenario in India and the following 
points be examined in light of current policies while developing the proposed blueprint:

5. The Committee notes that substantial physical infrastructure, encompassing laboratories, 
computational resources, and other facilities, coupled with robust institutional and administrative support, 
are indispensable for advancing science and engineering research. The operational expenses incurred in 
maintaining these essential facilities and cutting-edge research equipment are considerable. Internationally 
renowned universities cover these costs, including infrastructure development and maintenance, through 
overheads or indirect costs on research grants. The Committee, therefore, stresses that it is imperative by 
the concerned Ministries/ Departments to reconsider the overheads provided on public-funded research 
projects as the current rate falls significantly short of meeting the actual operational expenses which

institutions like IITs, Central Universities, and Higher Education Institutes to bolster their infrastructure 
and sustain high-quality research endeavours effectively.

Department of Higher Education 
I. Currently, 46 Central Universities are fully funded by the UGC. These grants are being provided 
for their overall development covering aspects like enhancing access, ensuring equity, imparting relevant 
education, improving quality, making the administration effective, enhancing facilities for students, 
augmenting research facilities and any other plans of universities. The financial assistance to the 
universities includes both Capital and Revenue (Salary and Recurring Expenditure) grants. These Central 
Universities have been engaged in research in diverse areas.  

35 
 
II.  The Ministry of Education releases funds to IITs as Grant-In-Aid for their recurring and non-
recurring expenditure from the scheme – ‘Support to IITs’ under three Heads viz. OH-35 (Capital), OH-
36 (Salary) and OH-31 (Other Recurring exp. Such as Pension, Scholarships, Administrative expenses 
etc.) In order to make the institutions self-sustainable in terms of taking up infrastructure/ capital 
activities, HEFA has been introduced. IITs are applying for loans through HEFA to strengthen their 
infrastructure. Further this department has also initiated the proposal for expansion of 3rd generation IITs. 
Department of Biotechnology 
This recommendation has been ‘NOTED’. It is submitted that Department of Biotechnology 
supports creation of research infrastructure in academic and research institutions across the country, 
through specific programs such as DBT-Boost to University Interdisciplinary Life science Departments 
for Education and Research programme (DBT-BUILDER) and DBT-Scientific Infrastructure Access for 
Harnessing Academia University Research Joint Collaboration (DBT-SAHAJ). 
Department of Science & Technology 
The recommendation has been noted by D/o Science & Technology. 
Comments/Observations of the Committee 
The Committee notes the initiatives taken by the Ministry of Education regarding release of 
funds for research activities in Higher Educational Institutions. The Committee is, however, of the 
view that steps should be taken to optimize resource utilisation/management and invest in 
sustainable and cost-effective research infrastructure building which would increase research 
funding availability and enhance research affordability thereby developing a sustainable research 
eco-system in the country. The Committee may be apprised of the steps taken by the Department of 
Biotechnology to bolster their research infrastructure and sustain high-quality research endeavours 
effectively. 
Recommendation  
6. The Committee notes the potential benefits of One Nation One Subscription (ONOS) initiative 
thereby promoting interdisciplinary research and its alignment with national policies like the National 
Education Policy 2020 (NEP), the draft Science Technology and Innovation Policy (STIP), and the vision 
of the National Research Foundation (NRF) in driving inclusive access to knowledge resources. The 
Committee strongly recommends the accelerated implementation of the One Nation One Subscription 
(ONOS) initiative to democratize access to scholarly publications and journals across all higher education 
and research institutions in India as access to scientific literature, primarily through digital journals, is 
currently hindered by exorbitant subscription costs and limited availability. 
(Para 6.14 of the 358th Report of the Committee) 
Action Taken 
Department of Higher Education 
I.  In order to facilitate inclusive access to knowledge resources, the INFLIBNET has launched e-
Shodh Sindhu, an online system that provides access to more than 10,000 e-journals and 8 lakhs e-books 
to more than 390 universities and more than 3800 colleges. 

36 
 
II.  One Nation One Subscription (ONOS) Scheme has been approved under which access to prized 
publications is provided to the needy Researchers at affordable cost. 
Department of Science & Technology 
Implementation of the ONOS is being coordinated by Office of the Principal Scientific Adviser to 
the Govt. of India. 
Department of Health Research 
This initiative is already being undertaken by PSA office and it is under consideration at ICMR 
Department of Agriculture Research & Education (ICAR) 
 Currently, Consortium for e-Resources in Agriculture (popularly known as CeRA) is an e-
Consortium of Agricultural Libraries under the Indian Council of Agricultural Research for National 
Agricultural Research and Education System (NARES) Libraries including State Agricultural 
Universities (SAUs), Central Agricultural Universities (CAUs), and Deemed Universities and ICAR 
institutes. As ONOS is implemented, CeRA e-resources would be merged in ONOS, ICAR would also be 
a part of this initiative and all e-resources subscribed under ONOS would be accessible to all Institutes 
and agricultural universities under NARES. 
Comments/Observations of the Committee 
The Committee notes that the ONOS scheme has been approved and implemented. The 
Committee’s recommendation had called for the accelerated implementation of the ONOS scheme. 
However, as the Committee noted in its 364th Report on Demand for Grants of the Higher 
Education Department (FY 24-25), about 4,000 of the 7,008 eligible institutions had still not 
received the benefits of the ONOS. The Committee would direct the Department to provide 
updated information on the current status of the ONOS’s reach, and provide an update on the steps 
taken to accelerate the scheme’s implementation. 
 
 
 

37 
 
CHAPTER-IV 
RECOMMENDATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF THE GOVERNMENT ARE 
STILL AWAITED 
Recommendation 
1.   The Committee strongly recommends for a comprehensive support framework from key 
Departments such as the Department of Higher Education and its subordinate bodies like UGC, AICTE 
and Departments of the Ministry of Science and Technology, extending their assistance to universities for 
the promotion and advancement of research in scientific and related fields. This support should 
encompass funding initiatives, active mentorship, guidance, and capacity-building measures to empower 
universities in their research endeavours. The Committee feels that these Departments can play a pivotal 
role in nurturing a robust research ecosystem across the academic landscape by actively catering to the 
needs of Universities. Initiatives such as targeted funding, guidance on best practices, and mentorship 
programs can significantly enhance the research capabilities and competitiveness of Universities to make 
them emerge and thrive as hubs of innovation, contributing meaningfully to the scientific and 
technological progress of the nation. 
(Para 6.13 of the 358th Report of the Committee) 
Action Taken 
Department of Higher Education 
I.   Research and innovation are essential aspects of enhancing quality education in Higher Education 
Institutions. Providing financial support for researchers through scholarships and fellowships is 
imperative and is undertaken by the UGC under various schemes. The Junior Research Fellowship 
(JRF) scheme of the University Grants Commission (UGC) is open to candidates who qualify in the 
National Eligibility Test-Junior Research Fellowship (NET-JRF) of the UGC and the UGC-Council of 
Scientific and Industrial Research (UGC-CSIR) joint test. 
 In order to extend assistance to universities for the promotion and advancement of research, the 
Information and Library Network (INFLIBNET), an Inter-University Centre (IUC) of UGC has 
developed and maintains Shodhganga- a reservoir of full-text online thesis contributed by HEIs. 
Shodhgangotri, another initiative by INFLIBNET, is a repository of Indian Research in Progress that 
hosts synopses /Major-Minor Research Projects (MRP)/Post-Doctoral Fellowship (PDF)/Emeritus 
Fellowship. Shodh-Chakra, another initiative of the INFLIBNET, provides a unique space to the 
researcher, guide/supervisor and university to manage the research lifecycle of a research scholar. This 
works as digital workspaces wherein researchers can collect, store, organize and cite their research work.  
 Further, under ShodhShuddhi, the Ministry of Education, Govt. of India has initiated a project to 
provide Plagiarism Detection Software (PDS) to all Indian Universities/ Institutions. 
II.  SPAs (School of Planning and Architecture) are willing to share their resources with Researchers. 
Department of Agriculture Research & Education (ICAR) 
● ICAR has been facilitating and supporting in the conduct of training programmes in the cutting 
edge areas of agriculture and allied sciences for the capacity building of the faculty, teachers and 
researchers in the National Agricultural Research, and Education System (NARES) comprising of ICAR 
Institutes and Agricultural Universities. This support is to enhance the competency level of Agricultural 

38 
 
faculty and to elevate the quality of agricultural education and research by offering advanced trainings 
across agricultural universities/ institutions. During last five years, 411 such training programmes have 
been organized benefitting 9688 participants.  
● Centres of Advanced Faculty Training (CAFT) are established across the country for undertaking 
discipline oriented advanced training for teaching, research and extension in cutting edge areas of 
agriculture and allied sciences for use in capabilities enhancement, educational innovations, modern 
teaching and research methodologies along with serving as repository of ideas and information in 
concerned disciplines. 
● ICAR promotes excellence in research by establishing and nurturing novel school of thought and 
developing strong centres of agricultural research and education around outstanding scientists through 
award of positions of National Professors and National Fellows. The contribution of National Professors 
and National Fellows in the form of technologies, patents, copyrights has immensely benefited the 
knowledge pool of the country. 
● The services of outstanding superannuated scientists/teachers from NARES in the form of 
Emeritus Scientists and Emeritus Professors are being utilized for supporting ongoing nationally 
important research, teaching specialized courses, developing quality instructional material for use in 
national agricultural education programme including distance education. The programme has helped to 
make use of the experience of retired professionals for remedying manpower imbalances in some of the 
crucial areas of research and teaching. This initiative aims to initiate new programmes in nationally 
important priority areas. 
Department of Biotechnology 
This recommendation has been ‘NOTED’. It is submitted that various programs of the Department 
support Universities for promotion and advancement of research in science. For example:  Junior Research 
Fellowship (JRF), Post Graduate Program,  Post-Doctoral Fellowship, Ramalingaswami Re-entry 
Fellowship etc. support high quality Post Graduate, PhD and Post-Doctoral Fellows to work in 
universities; the Star College, DBT-BUILDER and DBT-SAHAJ programs support development of 
scientific research infrastructure at College or University level.  
Additionally, teachers from universities are eligible to receive extra mural research grants to fulfill 
their research endeavors. Furthermore, research fellows and faculty members from universities are also 
supported to present research papers at international conferences and seminars through the Conference, 
Travel, Exhibition and Popular Lectures (CTEP) program of the Department. Though these initiatives, the 
Department has been playing pivotal role to nurture a robust research ecosystem in the Universities.  
Department of Scientific & Industrial Research 
The recommendation of committee is noted with thanks.  Department may like to submit that 
CSIR under its Capacity Building and Human Resource Development Schemes has been supporting two 
major programmes: (1) Extramural research Scheme and Emeritus Scientists; (2) Doctoral and 
Postdoctoral Fellowships in universities and affiliated colleges, institutions of national importance and 
R&D institutions including that of CSIR with the aim of promoting and advancement of research in 

39 
 
scientific & related field including engineering and technology, medical and pharmaceutical sciences. 
These schemes are playing a pivotal role in strengthening the capacity building of universities and grantee 
institutions and helping in mentorship of thousands of doctoral and postdoctoral young scientific talents.  
The specifics of these two programmes and their highlighted achievements are given hereunder: 
CSIR under its Capacity Building and Human Resource Development Scheme has implemented a 
programme “Extramural Research Scheme and Emeritus Scientist Scheme” promotes advancement of 
research in the fields of Science & Technology, including Agriculture, Engineering and Medicine and in 
inter- trans-disciplinary areas in academic and R&D institutions. Under this programme, CSIR provides 
research grants to superannuated outstanding scientists/academics. The financial grant is known as 
Emeritus Scientists grant which is given to superannuated researchers who wish to continue to pursue 
research in their respective fields of specializations in universities and R&D institutions and thereby 
contribute in strengthening institutional R&D capabilities, nurture young budding scientific talent and 
contributed in CSIR’s national efforts for human resource development. The experience of these 
superannuated scientists has proven a great help to the laboratories/academic institutions in carrying out 
some of the ongoing projects and mentoring the younger ones.  
Under the Extramural Research Scheme, research proposals from the universities and R&D 
institutions are funded in frontier areas of science and technology which are also in line with the research 
programme of CSIR laboratories. These extramural research schemes are beneficial towards building the 
R&D capabilities of the universities which in turn benefits the country in its scientific pursuits. It is worthy 
to apprise the committee that in the year 2023 on International Women’s Day 2023, a novel initiative was 
launched by CSIR under the auspices of the Hon’ble Minister of S&T (I/C), Dr Jitendra Singh where 
research grant proposals from only women scientists under the Extramural Research Scheme were invited.  
Accordingly, “A Special Call for Research Grants for Women Scientists (CSIR-ASPIRE)” was 
made by CSIR with the following objectives: 
● To align the Government of India’s initiative to empower women and promote ‘Nari Shakti’ in the 
country  
● To support the Hon’ble Prime Minister’s efforts to put Nari Shakti at the forefront of India’s 
development journey 
● To celebrate the Amrit Kal, CSIR for the first time in its history announced A Special Call for 
Research Grants for Women Scientists (CSIR-ASPIRE).  
The salient features of the CSIR-ASPIRE scheme are as follows: 
● The proposal to be supported invited from women scientists across the country. 
● Only women scientists across the country are eligible to apply for research grants to carry out 
R&D in major disciplines of science and engineering viz. Life Sciences, Chemical Sciences, 
Physical Sciences, Engineering Sciences and inter/trans disciplinary sciences.  
● The funds will be provided for staff (JRF/SRF/RA), contingency and equipment.  
● The total budget of a research proposal including research fellow’s stipend may be upto Rs. 
30 lacs.  
● The normal tenure of research proposal may be two or three years. 

40 
 
Additionally, at present CSIR has been supporting 850 Research Projects out which about 300 are 
funded to universities and colleges and rest in R&D institution including institutions of national 
importance to promote research in the fields of Science & Technology, including Agriculture, Engineering 
and Medicine and building the R&D capabilities of the universities and colleges.  
It is important to apprise here that majority (95-97%) of these extramural research projects are 
awarded to postgraduate colleges, deemed universities, State and Central universities, institution of 
National importance (IITs, IISc, IISERs, NITs) and other Higher Education Institutions (HEIs)  in the 
country.   
It is also important to apprise the Hon’ble Committee that CSIR under its Capacity Building and 
Human Resource Development: Doctoral and Postdoctoral Fellowship programme awards fellowships 
to young researchers to attract them to pursue doctoral and postdoctoral research in their subject domain in 
basic & applied sciences, engineering & technology and medicinal & Pharmaceutical sciences or in 
interdisciplinary & transdisciplinary area of research.  The young budding scientific talent undergoes 
extensive training in modern R&D methods in Science and technology followed in premier institutions 
across the globe under the mentorship of universities professors and scientists. The tenure of these 
fellowships varies from 3 years to 5 years.   
CSIR through Joint CSIR-UGC National Eligibility Test (NET) awards Junior Research 
Fellowship (JRF) for pursuing doctoral research in basic sciences and inter- & trans-disciplinary area of 
research. To promote academic excellence, the GATE qualified engineering graduates and GPAT 
qualified pharmaceutical graduates are provided JRF-GATE Fellowships to pursue research through a 
suitable PhD programme in AcSIR or in any other institution. CSIR also provides Senior Research 
Fellowships (SRF)-Direct to those young researchers who have postgraduate qualifications in science, 
engineering, and medicinal & pharmaceutical sciences, Trans-disciplinary area of research and Science 
and Technology Studies. CSIR also offers postdoctoral fellowships such as and Research Associateship 
(RA) and Senior Research Associateships (SRA) to PhD holders who have interests in science and 
technology research and are enthusiast about the advancement of their scientific career.  During 2021-22, 
2022-23 and 2023-24 the number of young researchers benefited from this programme “Capacity Building 
and Human Resource Development: Doctoral and Postdoctoral Fellowship Programmed” of CSIR are 
summarized in the table below:  
 2021-22 2022-23 2023-24 
Total number of research 
students benefitted 
10885 9185 7379 
 
Further to place on record, the major beneficiaries of the CSIR’s doctoral and postdoctoral 
fellowship programmes are Educational Institutions (Colleges, Deemed universities, State and Central 
universities, institutions of national importance (INI), and higher educational Institutions (HEIs)) as 
majority of the students (>65%) pursue their doctoral and postdoctoral research. 

41 
 
  The students, researchers & budding scientists while learning modern techniques and R&D 
methods under the mentorship of university professors and scientists, earn monthly stipend to support their 
studies and families. These young researchers contribute to scientific output particularly in research 
publications of high impact factor and it is also a fact that the research publications from an institute are 
directly co-related with the number of research fellows working in that institute. 
Recommendation 
 
2. The Committee appreciates the concerted efforts by various departments and institutes which has 
helped the IITs and IISCs to excel in World QS rankings. The Committee also appreciates the IISCs 
Bangalore for being ranked as the World’s Top Research University in terms of University Citation per 
Faculty in QS World Ranking 2022. 
(Para 6.20 of the 358th Report of the Committee) 
3. The Committee appreciates that India has witnessed a massive jump in its Global Innovation 
Index (GII) from 52nd in the year 2019 to 40th in the year 2023 among 132 economies of the world. Also 
its international research collaboration, especially in themes related to SDG 07 (Affordable and clean 
energy from 16% in 2018 to 20% in 2022). The Committee also appreciates the submission of the 
Department of Higher Education that the national spending on research and development (R&D) 
measured in terms of gross expenditure on Research and Development has increased over the years and 
more than doubled from Rs. 60,196.75 crore in 2010-11 to Rs. 1,27,380.96 crore in 2020-21 which is 
worth of appreciation. The Committee also appreciates the efforts of the Department of Higher Education 
for benchmarking Innovation and Entrepreneurship (I&E) ecosystem in higher education institutes (HEIs) 
through Atal Ranking of Institutions on Innovation Achievements (NIRF-Innovation) 
(Para 6.21 of the 358th Report of the Committee) 
4. Upon examining various Higher Education Institutes (HEIs) for future-readiness in the upcoming 
Industry 4.0 technologies such as Artificial Intelligence, Block Chain, Internet of Things (IoT), Quantum 
Technologies, etc., the Committee found their ongoing efforts in research, innovation and implementation 
of these future technologies to be satisfactory and on the right trajectory. 
(Para 6.22 of the 358th Report of the Committee) 
Action Taken 
Department of Higher Education and Department of Biotechnology 
The recommendation has been noted by D/o Higher Education and D/o Biotechnology.

***** 
 
Comments/Observations of the Committee 
1. The Committee appreciates the actions/steps taken by the Department of Higher Education, 
University Grants Commission (UGC), All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE) and 
Department of Science and Technology in identifying key national priorities, emerging frontiers 
and strategic research areas, practically addressing the endeavors of funding the scientific research 
and aligning them with the objectives of the Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF).  
The Committee also notes that the Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF) Act,
